events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. (https://classes.berkeley.edu/content/2022-fall-histart-37-001-lec-001) Co-sponsored by the Institute for South Asia Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (http://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/), and the South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/initiatives/SAAI) at UC Berkeley. —DATES: Sept 9��Dec 13, 2026 VENUE: BAMPFA HOURS: Wed-Sun, 11 AM–7 PM (Mon and Tues closed) TICKETS: Buy tickets HERE (https://bampfa.org/visit/hours) ��———————- Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952). events.title: Exhibit | Centering Philippine and Filipinx American Histories: Selections from The Bancroft Library
events.description: The Bancroft Library's collections of materials relating to the Philippines span nearly 500 years. Highlights in this exhibit include a transcript of an Inquisitorial trial from 1646, a prayer book written in the Cebuano language, and UC Berkeley Filipino student publications from 1905 to the present. The exhibit also features selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author Jessica Hagedorn, including typewritten drafts of her novels, poetry, song lyrics, and a screenplay, as well as childhood drawings and writings.Bancroft's renowned Latin American collections offer up intriguing examples of documents produced by the Spanish Empire as it exploited the islands' natural, cultural, and human resources. Examples include the transcript of the Inquisitorial trial of two women accused of being spiritual mediums, a manuscript written in the Jawi script, which is based on Arabic script promising religious freedom to the Muslim residents of the island of Mindanao, and materials regarding the trade between Manila and Mexico.The personal papers and published works of UC Berkeley professors Bernard Moses (1846-1931) and David Barrows (1873-1954) document their early involvement with American colonialism in the Philippines, especially their work in redesigning the Filipino education system. In the aftermath of a brutal war, Americans viewed education as a tool for pacifying a conquered population. Documentation of these professors' white supremacist views is contrasted with the work of Filipinx and Asian American scholars who use their words to critique colonialism and its racist underpinnings.Educational opportunities have brought students from the Philippines, and later Filipinx American students, to Berkeley since the early 20th century. The exhibit includes examples of four student publications — two published in the first two decades of the 1900s and two more contemporary examples — that provide evidence of these students' political engagement and their determination to make their voices heard.Selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author and performance artist Jessica Hagedorn are also on display, including examples of her novels, plays, poetry, song lyrics, a screenplay, childhood drawings, and writings. Hagedorn employs a kaleidoscope of pop culture references, songs, images, and quotes from historical figures, and a galaxy of characters representing various cultures, classes, genders, races, and nationalities in her depictions of the Philippines and Filipinx America.Open hours may vary. Please view the The Bancroft Library hours (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/bancroft) page for the most up-to-date information.

events.description: The exhibit features highlights from The Bancroft Library's extensive collection of prints. events.title: Exhibit | Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley
events.location: The Rowell Exhibition Cases, Doe Library, 2nd floor
events.description: In 1985, UC Berkeley students, with support from faculty, staff, and labor unions, transformed the campus into the heart of a powerful anti-apartheid divestment campaign. They organized rallies, teach-ins, and shantytown encampments to protest the university's financial ties to companies profiting from South Africa's system of racial segregation. Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley highlights a movement that mobilized thousands, politicized a new generation, and laid the groundwork for ongoing struggles for racial and economic justice.

events.title: Exhibit | Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Bernice Layne Brown Gallery (inside Doe Library)
events.description: In August 2023, thirty international artists, writers, scientists, and filmmakers traveled 450 nautical miles across the Marshall Islands with youth and elders from the nation's Indigenous communities. That expedition, Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here (https://www.ourlifeishere.org), was not one to witness ruin, but a return: an act of honoring ancestral lands, the struggles of those who came before, and the enduring presence of Marshallese life today. An exhibition in Doe Library's Bernice Layne Brown Gallery gathers reproductions of works made during and after the voyage together with rare books, maps, and photographs drawn from UC Berkeley's own libraries—The Bancroft Library, the Earth Sciences & Map Library, the Environmental Design Library, Morrison Library, and the Main (Gardner) Stacks. Six cases move from the conditions that shaped the voyage, through the journey itself, to the living Marshallese knowledge and youth-led activism that carry it forward. Interpretive text is punctuated by QR codes linking to films, poems, and the organizations at the center of the project. This presentation is part of a series of exhibitions, installations, courses, and public programs across UC Berkeley during the 2026–27 academic year (https://cici.berkeley.edu/komij-mour-ijin-our-life-here-uc-berkeley), guided by the Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative. The exhibition was co-curated by independent curators Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll, in partnership with UC Berkeley librarians Becky Miller and Susan Powell. The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell.

events.title: Exhibition: "Hidden Layers: AI Infrastructures and Hallucinations"
events.location: Worth Ryder Art Gallery, Anthropology & Art Building, Rm 116
events.description: The Department of German and the Department of Art Practice are excited to announce the opening of Hidden Layers: AI Infrastructures and Hallucinations, curated by Antonio Somaini with Hannes Bajohr and Sonja Thiel, in dialogue with the France–Berkeley research initiative The Latent Spaces of Culture, and on display at the Worth Ryder Art Gallery. This exhibition examines some of the concealed dimensions of contemporary AI culture — the planetary infrastructures of extraction and computation, the often invisible human labor, the latent vector spaces within which culture is compressed and processed, and the models' hallucinations. Hidden Layers tackles these phenomena from two different perspectives: AI Infrastructures and AI Hallucinations. Featuring works by Nouf Aljowaysir; Gašper and Nina Beguš & Metahaven; Grégory Chatonsky; Kate Crawford & Vladan Joler; Asma Kazmi & Jill Miller; Andrea Khôra; Occitane Lacurie & Barnabé Sauvage; Greg Niemeyer; and Mario Santamaria & Alex Saum-Pascual. The project is a collaboration between the Department of German and the Worth Ryder Art Gallery at the Department of Art Practice.Exhibition Dates: September 3 - October 3, 2026Opening Reception: Thursday, September 3, 4-6:30pm, Worth Ryder Art Gallery RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSd_OOMe7YQHw3CYbSr673UCSlQ0f4mn4lZ7g46KhRUTRpC5qQ/viewform?usp=dialog)Artist Talk, Gregory Chatonsky: Thursday, September 3, 6:30-8:00pm, AAPB 285 RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSd_OOMe7YQHw3CYbSr673UCSlQ0f4mn4lZ7g46KhRUTRpC5qQ/viewform?usp=dialog)Related programming:Film Program: September 9, 7 pm, BAMPFAWorkshop on Latent Spaces of Culture: September 9, 2pm-4pm; September 10/11, 9:30 am-4pm on both days, 470 Stephens Additional events and more details to be announced. Times subject to change, please also check the campus calendar. This exhibition is supported by the France-Berkeley Fund of the Institute of European Studies, the Department of German and the Department of Art Practice, together with the Berkeley Center for New Media, the Berkeley Institute for Data Science (BIDS), Department of Rhetoric; Antikythera, the Pamela P. Fong and Family Distinguished Chair in China Studies, the Division of Arts & Humanities, the Townsend Center for the Humanities and the School of Information, the Technology Network of the Berkeley Economy and Society Initiative (BESI); and the Berkeley Art, Law, and Finance Project, hosted by the Berkeley Center for Law and Business at Berkeley Law. In conjunction with the exhibition, additional programming is developed in collaboration with Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) and the Institute for Contemporary Art San Jose.

events.title: Photography Installation: Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands
events.description: At Giannini Hall, 36 photographs selected from the recently published Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands (Radius Books, © 2026) by Mark Klett and William L. Fox extend the two men's decades-long collaboration tracing the nuclear history of the American West and the broader Pacific sphere. Installed along the building's main hallway, the images move between the physical remains of nuclear testing—bunkers, craters, camera towers reclaimed by jungle—and the everyday textures of Marshallese life: canoe building, weaving, seawalls raised by hand. Paired with archival images from the testing era and drawn from Fox's field notes and essays, the photo essay holds both histories at once: the violence of nuclear history, and the resilience of a culture that continues to inhabit these islands. An artist and curator-led tour with Mark Klett and William L. Fox will take place on September 23 at 4 PM. —Mark Klett is a photographer interested in the intersection of places, history and time. His background includes working as a geologist before turning to photography. Klett has received fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation, the Pollock-Krasner Foundation, the National Endowment for the Arts, and the Japan/US Friendship Commission. His work has been exhibited and published widely in the United States and internationally, and is held in over eighty museum collections worldwide. He is the author/co-author of twenty books. Klett is Regents' Professor Emeritus at Arizona State University where he taught for forty years. —Presented by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative in partnership with the Rausser College of Natural Resources.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation. —Image Credit: "The concrete bunker destroyed by the 15-megaton Bravo explosion"2023. events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. Exhibition Team:Lauren Graves, Guest CuratorAlissa Schapiro and Hannah Weisman, Coordinating CuratorsAndrea Calderon, RegistrarDavid Sullivan, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Special thanks to Michael S. Sachs, who has made this exhibition possible through his generous gift of Nancy Lee Katz's Pantheon (2024.1), loan of additional prints, and gracious consultations. events.title: Exhibit | Time Capsules: Exploring the Permanent Collection (copy)
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. These exhibitions relied on its extensive, and ever-growing, holdings of art, books, manuscripts, and material culture, as well as different modalities in which these materials can be studied and displayed: from curatorial and scholarly forays into the collection to research projects created in collaboration with UC Berkeley Graduate and Undergraduate students, to real-life experiments with ideas borne out of courses and seminars. Each exhibition featured in Time Capsules is unique in exploring the cultures of the Jews in a global perspective, in bringing museum objects "back to life," and in offering ever-changing ways to understand the past in order to inform the future.Exhibition Team:Francesco Spagnolo and Shir Gal Kochavi, CuratorsZoe Foster, Undergraduate Curatorial ApprenticeJulie Franklin, RegistrarErnest Jolly, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Located in downtown Berkeley, just steps from campus, the museum and research center is home to one of the world's preeminent collections of Jewish art and life. The Magnes generates new knowledge and understanding of Jewish cultures with and for its academic and public audiences through its collections-based exhibitions and programs. events.title: Lunch Poems: Rowan Ricardo Phillips
events.description: Lunch Poems (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/lunch-poems), Berkeley's storied noontime poetry series, welcomes Rowan Ricardo Phillips. Rowan Ricardo Phillips is the author of four books of poems — The Ground, Heaven, Living Weapon, and Silver — and two books of prose, When Blackness Rhymes with Blackness and The Circuit: A Tennis Odyssey. A fifth collection, The Milky Way, is forthcoming from Farrar, Straus and Giroux. His honors include a Whiting Award, a Guggenheim Fellowship, the Anisfield-Wolf Book Award for poetry, the PEN/ESPN Award for Literary Sports Writing, and an Arts and Letters Award in literature from the American Academy of Arts and Letters. He is the poetry editor of The New Republic and the editor of the Princeton Series of Contemporary Poets. He also translates from Catalan. He is presidential professor and distinguished professor of English at Stony Brook University. He lives in New York and Barcelona. The Lunch Poems series, founded by Professor Robert Hass, is supported by Dr. and Mrs. Tom Colby, the UC Berkeley Library, the Morrison Library Fund, the UC Berkeley English Department, and the Deans' Office of the College of Letters & Science. For more information or to be added to the Lunch Poems mailing list, please email poems-library@berkeley.edu (mailto:poems-library@berkeley.edu) or follow @PoemsLunch on Instagram (http://instagram.com/poemslunch) and X (https://twitter.com/PoemsLunch).

events.title: Are We Living in a 1938 Moment? How Autocracies Threaten the West
events.description: Are We Living in a 1938 Moment? How Autocracies Threaten the West Thursday, October 1, 12:30 – 2 pm *Lunchtime talk* Institute of International Studies 223 Philosophy HallREGISTER (https://forms.gle/aJvKjMEtZbCn3H1JA)The warning signs of the 1930s feel alarmingly familiar today: nationalist rhetoric, revisionism, military rearmament, political polarization. The liberal order is eroding, autocracies are rearming, and the West appears weaker than at any point in decades. In this book talk, historian and security expert Dr. Moritz Pöllath argues that these patterns function as an early warning system for the present: a new authoritarian axis — Russia, China, North Korea, Iran — is forming, exploiting a strategic power vacuum to impose a world order beyond freedom and democracy. The years ahead may prove decisive: between 2027 and 2030, the world may decide whether it descends into a new global systemic conflict, with a possible attack on Taiwan as its most dangerous flashpoint. Moritz Pöllath is an Assistant Professor of Public History at Ludwig Maximilian University Munich, where he teaches courses on the History of Democracy, US History, the Cold War, and history teaching methods for secondary schools. He studied Diplomatic and Military History at Hawaiʻi Pacific University and American History at the University of Cologne. His first book, Out-of-Area? NATO and Decolonization in Africa and Asia 1949–1961 (2017), explores the roots of NATO's global security policy during the early Cold War; his second book (habilitation), Narrating Freedom: Challenges to American and German Master Narratives in the 21st Century, was completed in 2023. He has held visiting professorships at the University of Leipzig and was previously a visiting scholar at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a fellow of the Cold War Studies Program at Harvard University and the University of Udine.

events.title: Black Feminism & The Issue of Practice
events.location: Maude Fife Room, 315 Wheeler Hall, UC Berkeley
events.description: Please RSVP to attend (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScBDQrjMuo76n6pZySYpqe58aLn5PGOzcfC-UsmeoIXwLOYeg/viewform?usp=publish-editor). Join the Banned Scholars Project and A Counter-Imaginary in Authoritarian Times for a conversation with scholars Keeanga-Yamahtta Taylor and Sarah Haley. Responding to the move to reduce Black feminism to an analytic, Taylor and Haley will trace its genealogies and practices as a guide for political struggle. How can the tools of Black feminism and the legacy of radical Black left feminists inform resistance in our current moment and authoritarian times?Keeanga-Yamahtta Taylor writes and speaks on Black politics, social movements, and racial inequality in the United States. ​She is author Race for Profit: How Banks and the Real Estate Industry Undermined Black Homeownership, published in 2019 by University of North Carolina Press. Race for Profit was a semi-finalist for the 2019 National Book Award and a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize in History in 2020. She is a 2021 MacArthur Foundation Fellow. Her earlier book From #BlackLivesMatter to Black Liberation won the Lannan Cultural Freedom Award for an Especially Notable Book in 2016. She is also editor of How We Get Free: Black Feminism and the Combahee River Collective, which won the Lambda Literary Award for LGBQT nonfiction in 2018, and co-editor with Colin Kaepernick and Robin D.G. Kelley of Our History Has Always Been Contraband: In Defense of Black Studies.Sarah Haley's research areas include African American and queer history, feminist historical methods, carceral history, and prison abolition. She is the author of No Mercy Here: Gender, Punishment, and the Making of Jim Crow Modernity. She organizes with Scholars for Social Justice and is director of the Institute for the Study of Sexuality and Gender at Columbia University.

events.title: Chases, clusters, and surfin' birds: Effects of group flight on locomotor biomechanics and energetics
events.description: Context matters in locomotion biomechanics, through direct effects such as differences in terrain or the environment altering the physics of locomotion, and indirectly when different contexts alter the underlying trade-offs between different approaches to movement. Group or collective movement represents one such context and here I use field recordings and laboratory experiments to explore how group interactions affect fundamental aspects of locomotor biomechanics and energetics in bird flight. Specific examples include tandem flights in Cliff Swallows, the cluster flocks of shorebird species across a range of body sizes, and an experimental wind tunnel examination of the energetics of European Starlings flying solo and in small groups. These specific examples demonstrate the importance of group movement context in bird flight while also suggesting similar context-driven changes in other organisms, in other environments, and during other behaviors.

events.title: CCB Seminar: Markus Covert - The E. coli Whole-Cell Modeling Project: Accelerating Discovery via Comprehensive Biological Simulation
events.description: Abstract: Francis Crick first called for a coordinated worldwide scientific effort to determine a "complete solution" of the bacterium Escherichia coli. We have been working for some years now to complete a model of E. coli that takes into account all of the known functions of every well-annotated gene, in order to better understand and predict the behavior of this scientifically-relevant and industrially-significant model organism. Now that a majority of the annotated gene functions have been added to the model, our simulations have generated biological insights that change our perspectives about cellular biology and physiology. As examples, I will present our new findings regarding how metals are utilized in E. coli, as well as the effect of gene organization into operons, and the impact of engineering new gene content into the chromosome.Bio: Markus Covert is the Ram Shriram Chair and Professor of Bioengineering at Stanford University. Over the course of his career, his lab has generated several new exciting technologies to measure, analyze, and mathematically model the behaviors of individual cells. The lab is probably best known for constructing the first "whole-cell" computational model, which explicitly represents all known gene functions and molecules in a bacterial cell - an advance which was highlighted by the journal Cell as a highlight publication of the 40-year history of that journal. Markus is the author of the textbook Fundamentals of Systems Biology: from Synthetic Circuits to Whole-Cell Models. He has received several awards for his efforts to develop new technologies, in particular the NIH Director's Pioneer Award, and the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation Distinguished Investigator and Discovery Center awards. He has also consulted in industry, including on the scientific advisory board of Emerald Cloud Labs, and as an inaugural Ambassador at X Labs, (previously Google [X]). Finally, Markus has taught one of the most popular courses at Stanford for several years, an integrated "lecture, lab and lunch" course entitled Bon Appétit, Marie Curie! The Science of Haute Cuisine.

events.title: Astronomy Colloquium - Andrew Mummery (IAS)
events.description: Title: Black holes, disks and jets: understanding the multi wavelength world of tidal disruption eventsAbstract: When unfortunate stars are scattered sufficiently close to a massive black hole they can be ripped apart, in their entirety, by tidal forces. These so-called tidal disruption events (TDEs) power multi wavelength flares which promise to offer insight into a wide range of questions in contemporary astrophysics, including the evolution, stability, and scale invariance of black hole accretion, the physics of jet launching, and black hole demographics (among many more). I will first discuss recent advances in our understanding of transient black hole accretion physics, before showing how this understanding allows us to maximize the utility of current and forthcoming multi wavelength TDE data sets. I will show that the optical TDE sample discovered by ZTF allows us to add ~50 low mass black holes to the M-sigma diagram, while the LSST survey will lead to of order ~1000 systems being added, revolutionizing our understanding of black hole growth and feedback at the lowest mass scales. Turning to accretion physics, I will discuss how by combining radio, optical and X-ray data sets we can answer old questions regarding the scale invariance of the accretion process, and contemporary questions regarding disk warping.Host: Ryan Chornock

events.title: Authors Meet Critics: "Demos: How the People Ruled Athens"
events.description: REGISTER (https://forms.gle/KddCT6ubaNBAkJXY8) Join us on October 1 for an Authors Meet Critics panel on the book Demos: How the People Ruled Athens, by Daniela Cammack, Assistant Professor of Political Science at UC Berkeley, with a courtesy appointment in the Department of Ancient Greek and Roman Studies (formerly Classics). Professor Cammack will be joined in conversation by James Porter, Distinguished Professor and Irving Stone Chair in Literature in the Department of Rhetoric at UC Berkeley, and Kinch Hoekstra, Chancellor's Professor of Political Science and Law at UC Berkeley. This event is co-sponsored by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Departments of Political Science and Ancient Greek & Roman Studies. The Social Science Matrix Authors Meet Critics (https://matrix.berkeley.edu/category/event-type/authors-meet-critics/) book series features lively discussions about recently published books authored by social scientists at UC Berkeley. For each event, the author discusses the key arguments of their book with fellow scholars. These events are free and open to the public.About the Book In ancient Greece, demokratia meant "rule by the people"—but what people, and how did they rule? Scholars have long argued that demokratia signified the rule of all adult male citizens over themselves. In Demos, Daniela Cammack counters this view by arguing that demokratia meant rule by the crowd that assembled when a public meeting was held. This crowd was the demos, which the Greeks distinguished from orators, generals, councilors, public benefactors, and other civic leaders. Drawing on literary and epigraphical evidence as well as the key theoretical insights of Aristotle and Hobbes, Cammack explains how constantly changing masses of ordinary ancient Greek men ruled while their leaders were ruled over. This political system relied on kratos, the power to prevail militarily, epitomized by the victories of the Athenian demos in civil conflicts around 508 and 404 BC. In peacetime, the superior strength of the demos revealed itself in large, frequently summoned crowds of ordinary citizens acting as policymakers, legislators, and (crucially) judges, who wielded great power over politicians. Aristotle characterized the years 403 to 322 as the era of "ultimate democracy," and it was during this period that the Athenians pulled off a feat unmatched by modern democrats: making use of talented and ambitious leaders without being ruled by them. By contrast, the Greeks called rule by elected office-holders "oligarchy." As people today lose faith in democratic institutions, Cammack's account prompts us to ask if we've been doing democracy all wrong—or even at all.PanelistsDaniela Cammack (https://polisci.berkeley.edu/people/person/daniela-cammack) is Assistant Professor of Political Science, affiliated with the Department of Ancient Greek and Roman Studies. She teaches broadly in the history of political thought and has particularly well-developed research interests in ancient Greek political thought, the history and theory of democracy, ancient and modern. and the topics of crowd power, deliberation, representation, and demotic sovereignty. She holds a B.A. in Modern History and English Literature (2002) from Oxford, an M.Phil. in Political Theory and Intellectual History (2005) from Cambridge, and a Ph.D. in Political Theory (2013) from Harvard, where her dissertation, Rethinking Athenian Democracy, won Harvard's Noxon Toppan Prize for the best dissertation in Political Science. Before moving to Berkeley in 2019, she was a Junior Fellow in Harvard's Society of Fellows and an Assistant Professor at Yale. Over the past decade, she has published numerous book chapters and articles in journals including Political Theory, The Journal of Political Philosophy, The Journal of Politics, and Classical Quarterly; she is also executive co-editor of History of Political Thought and associate editor of Polis, the Journal for Ancient Greek and Roman Political Thought. Her book, Demos: How the People Ruled Athens, will be published in January 2027 by Princeton University Press. A sequel, entitled Democracy: How the People Lost Power, is in progress and also under contract with Princeton. Kinch Hoestra (https://polisci.berkeley.edu/people/person/kinch-hoekstra) is Chancellor's Professor of Political Science and Law at UC Berkeley. He works on the history of political, moral, and legal thought, especially ancient, renaissance, and early modern political philosophy. Recent contributions to ancient political thought include "Athenian Democracy and Popular Tyranny," "Thucydides and the Politics of Necessity" (with Mark Fisher), and "The Liberties of the Ancients" (with Quentin Skinner). Another focus of Hoestra's research has been the philosophy of Thomas Hobbes (including studies of his theory of equality, obligation, democracy, tyranny, mixed government, natural law, and the rationality of justice); he co-edited The Oxford Handbook of Hobbes. Work that bridges these two areas includes "Hobbes and Aristotle on the Foundation of Political Science" (with Nicholas Gooding), "Hobbes's Thucydides", "Thucydides in the Renaissance and Reformation", and "The Melian Dilemma". From 1996 to 2007, he was a member of the Faculty of Philosophy at the University of Oxford, where he regularly taught graduate students in the Faculty of Classics and the Department of Politics and International Relations.James Porter (https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/faculty/james-porter) is Irving Stone Professor in Literature and Distinguished Professor in Rhetoric. His teaching and research has followed a few different trajectories. One is a study of Nietzsche's thought, early and late (Nietzsche and the Philology of the Future and The Invention of Dionysus: An Essay on 'The Birth of Tragedy' (both Stanford University Press, 2000). Another is a study of models of aesthetic sensation, perception, and experience in ancient Greece and Rome, which he explored in The Origins of Aesthetic Thought in Ancient Greece: Matter, Sensation, and Experience (Cambridge University Press, 2010; pbk. 2016). A continuation of this inquiry is The Sublime in Antiquity (Cambridge University Press, 2016; pbk. 2020), which received the C. J. Goodwin Award of Merit from The Society for Classical Studies (2017). A further strand is Jewish literary and critical thought in authors from Spinoza to Freud, Adorno, and Arendt. His most recent book is Homer: The Very Idea (University of Chicago Press, 2021; pbk. 2023), which captures some of his interest in classical reception studies. Current projects include Existence, Crisis, and Faith: Selected Essays and Letters by Rachel Bespaloff, a Cambridge Critical Guide to The Birth of Tragedy (co-edited with Michael Forster), and The Cynics: A Very Short Introduction. Dylan Riley (https://sociology.berkeley.edu/faculty/dylan-john-riley) studies capitalism, socialism, democracy, authoritarianism, and knowledge regimes in a broad comparative and historical perspective. His first book, The Civic Foundations of Fascism in Europe: Italy, Spain, and Romania 1870-1945 (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2010), argues that fascist regimes arose paradoxically on the basis of strong civil societies in the pre-fascist period. Reviewers have called this book "the most original and provocative new analysis of the preconditions of Fascism that has appeared in years", and "brilliant and courageous". A second book, How Societies and States Count: A Comparative Genealogy of Censuses (with Rebecca Jean Emigh and Patricia Ahmed in preparation for Palgrave), argues, against state centered accounts of official information that censuses work best where there is intense interaction between state and society. He has started a new project investigating the connection between the meaning and substance of democracy in interwar and post-war Europe. Riley has also published articles in the American Journal of Sociology, American Sociological Review, Catalyst, Comparative Studies in Society and History, Comparative Sociology, Social Science History, The Socio-Economic Review, and the New Left Review. He is a member of the editorial committee of the New Left Review.

events.title: Seminar 242, Econometrics Seminar: Lihua Lei (Stanford University) - Estimating Many Binomial Means
events.description: Many applications involve estimating the mean of multiple binomial outcomes as a com- mon problem – assessing intergenerational mobility of census tracts, estimating prevalence of infectious diseases across countries, and measuring click-through rates for different demo- graphic groups. The most standard approach is to report the plain average of each outcome. Despite simplicity, the estimates are noisy when the sample sizes or mean parameters are small. In contrast, the Empirical Bayes (EB) methods are able to boost the average accu- racy by borrowing information across tasks. Nevertheless, the EB methods require a Bayesian model where the parameters are sampled from a prior distribution which, unlike the commonly- studied Gaussian case, is unidentified due to discreteness of binomial measurements. Even if the prior distribution is known, the computation is difficult when the sample sizes are hetero- geneous as there is no simple joint conjugate prior for the sample size and mean parameter. In this paper, we consider the compound decision framework which treats the sample size and mean parameters as fixed quantities. We develop an approximate Stein's Unbiased Risk Estimator (SURE) for the average mean squared error given any class of estimators. For a class of machine learning-assisted linear shrinkage estimators, we establish asymptotic optimality, regret bounds, and valid inference. Unlike existing work, we work with the binomials directly without resorting to Gaussian approximations. This allows us to work with small sample sizes and/or mean parameters in both one-sample and two-sample settings. We demonstrate our approach using three datasets on firm discrimination, education outcomes, and innovation rates. Full paper here (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.25042).

events.title: Mathematics Department Colloquium: The arithmetic of differential equations
events.description: Speaker: Daniel Litt, University of TorontoIn 1875 Fuchs asked for a criterion that determines when the solutions to an algebraic differential equation are themselves algebraic functions. Conjectural answers to this question have been given by Grothendieck and Katz, Ekedahl–Shepherd-Barron–Taylor, and Bost, in terms of the arithmetic of the differential equation's structure constants. I'll explain joint work in progress with Joshua Lam verifying these conjectures for a class of non-linear differential equations arising in algebraic geometry. This work is largely an excuse to try to better understand the arithmetic and geometry of algebraic differential equations and representations of fundamental groups of algebraic varieties.

events.title: Miroslav Krleza, "Foreword to Krsto Hegedusic's The Drava Valley Motifs" (NYS reading group)
events.location: Event held at Stanford (Berkeley carpool meets at Dwinelle Roundabout at 4pm)
events.description: The next session of the Berkeley-Stanford New Yugoslav Studies group is held on Thursday, Oct 1, at Stanford (Building 260, Room 252). The session will focus on the writings of Miroslav Krle��a, maybe the figure who looms largest in all of Yugoslav literature. Krleža laid a foundation for what Yugoslav culture would look like even before the founding of socialist Yugoslavia. Starting in the late 1920s, he entered into a spirited argument – now known as the "Conflict on the Literary Left" (Sukob na književnoj ljevici) – about the relationship between beauty, ideology, and political commitment in art. We'll read two texts by Krleža for next Thursday: First, we'll read an essay he wrote in 1933 as the Preface to the collection Podravski motivi(The Drava Valley Motifs) by the artist Krsto Hegedušić. An important statement of Krleža's views about art and socialism, this essay was also written against the Soviet program of "socialist realism." Secondly, we'll jump from the interwar period into the early years of socialist Yugoslavia, and read Krleža's Speech at the 1952 Writers' Congress in Ljubljana. This speech is a major historical document, as well as a pleasure to read: it's usually seen as the definitive public statement of socialist Yugoslavia's policy of variety and experimentation in the arts, the cultural equivalent of Yugoslavia's geopolitical non-alignment and split with both the Soviet Union and the capitalist world.* Note that this NYS session is taking place at Stanford (Pigott 252) at 6pm. Carpool from Berkeley meets at 4pm at the roundabout behind Dwinelle Hall. For readings and to join the NYS carpool, contact Djordje Popovic (dpopovic@berkeley.edu (mailto:dpopovic@berkeely.edu)). Contact person at Stanford: Dominick Lawton (dlawton@stanford.edu (mailto:dlawton@stanford.edu))

events.title: Panel Discussion: Water and AI
events.location: Anthropology and Art Practice Building, Room 120
events.description: The Water and AI panel brings together four speakers with different answers to a simple question: What is water? For Tiah Ross-Butner, a UC Berkeley student and enrolled member of the Yurok Tribe, water is family. For Dr. Sheena Conforti, a Stanford researcher who studies wastewater and public health, water carries information about community health. For Dr. Suzanne Pierre, water is contamination, a force that spreads pollution deep into the soil. For Dr. Lance Legel, a UC Berkeley visiting scientist who uses AI to study ecosystems, water is a resource we need to understand more deeply. For Greg Niemeyer, a UC Berkeley professor and data artist, water is circulation. For Vivien Slagle, a UC Berkeley student studying art, anthropology, and law, water is a shared resource under competing demands from agriculture, data centers, and living systems. Water also helps make AI possible. Many data centers use water for cooling, and producing the electricity they consume can require additional water. Together, the panelists will explore how their cultures and practices shape the ways we understand and talk about water, and how these conversations can support sustainable water management. What is water? How can we talk across our differences? And where can we find common ground? This event is sponsored by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative.

events.title: Film Screening: Italianamerican and American Boy: A Profile of Steven Prince
events.description: Martin Scorsese's documentaries are like portals to his sources of inspiration, and Italianamerican takes us to the heart of the matter via a conversation with his parents. As his mother prepares meatballs, she and her husband tell the stories of their families' journeys from Sicily to Elizabeth Street, which speak volumes about the immigrant experience. American Boy is the realization of Scorsese's idea for a film in which "a man sits down, tells his story, and little by little you see an era emerge, a way of life, a way of surviving." He found the perfect subject in Steven Prince, a great storyteller, who played the gun dealer in Taxi Driver, a role for which he provided his own guns.

events.description: The Berkeley Tamil Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/language/berkeley-tamil-initiative) is pleased to present The Work of Form in Tamil Narrative Cultures (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/language/tamilberkeley/uc-berkeley-conference-tamil-studies), a Tamil Studies conference exploring vaṭivam—form, shape, style, arrangement, and embodiment—as a way to understand how Tamil narratives are created, circulated, and transformed across literature, performance, visual culture, cinema, and digital media. More than a neutral vessel for narrative, vaṭivam offers a way to understand form as an aesthetic practice, a material structure, and a response to changing social worlds. Bringing together scholars working across literature, performance, visual culture, cinema, and digital media, the conference will examine how Tamil narrative forms have been made and remade across time. By placing premodern and modern materials in conversation, The Work of Form in Tamil Narrative Cultures (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/language/tamilberkeley/uc-berkeley-conference-tamil-studies) asks how Tamil traditions can contribute to broader debates on form, media, and circulation, while remaining attentive to the histories, languages, and material contexts that shape Tamil cultural production. events.title: Defending Democracy Online Through Social Media: Deep Fakes and Our Cognitive Security, with Alexa Koenig
events.description: Digital technologies are rapidly transforming how people live their lives, including their access to information. Social media and smartphones are affecting both the creation and consumption of news — trapping consumers in information "silos" that obscure alternate points of view — while deep fakes are threatening the quality of information found online. All of this raises significant risks for the functioning of our democracy. Dr. Alexa Koenig will discuss this new information environment, some of the challenges it poses for democracy — including our sense of cognitive security — and opportunities for uncovering the truth in this digital age.About the Speaker Dr. Alexa Koenig is faculty director of Berkeley's MacArthur-Award Winning Human Rights Center; co-founder of U.C. Berkeley's Investigations Lab; and a research professor at Berkeley Law, where she focuses on the role of new and emerging technologies in human rights research and investigation.

events.title: Dissertation Talk: Frequency Synthesis for Integrated FMCW Sensing and Communication
events.description: Frequency-modulated continuous wave (FMCW) radar is an attractive solution for wireless sensing of distance and velocity, enabling fine resolution and simple receiver design. The critical determinant of the performance of an FMCW radar system is the linear FM "chirp" used as both the transmitted signal and the frequency-translator of received echos. In particular, chirp nonidealities, including FM nonlinearity and phase noise, create artifacts in the intermediate frequency (IF) spectrum which directly constrain the signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio (SNDR). In this talk, I will present the two-phase "chart & chirp" method of one-shot, in situ voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) tuning curve estimation and learning ("chart") with on-demand predistortion ("chirp") for all physically realizable chirp parameters. Using a cycle-counting frequency-to-digital converter (FDC) in the "chart" phase and an integrating digital-to-analog converter (QDAC) providing linear voltage interpolation in the "chart" phase, this architecture produces optimally linear chirps via linear least-squares estimation (LLSE). Analysis and simulation of the FM and phase errors of generated chirps in the time- and frequency-domains reveal deterministic links between chirp nonlinearity and artifacts in the IF spectrum, including ghost targets and spectral smearing. Remarkably, these results demonstrate the possibility for poor IF SNDR in spite of low RMS FM error and phase noise, and I will discuss the modulation parameters necessary for high IF SNDR and accurate target detection.

events.title: BETR/EECS Solid State Technologies Seminar: Thrinadh Dasyam & Christina Schuler, Intel | How Do You Find a Bug in a Billion-Transistor Chip?
events.description: Abstract: Modern System-on-Chip (SoC) designs contain billions of transistors and integrate processors, memory controllers, high-speed interfaces, security engines, and many other complex components. With this level of complexity, how do engineers find a tiny design bug before the chip is manufactured? This presentation introduces the fascinating world of Design Verification (DV) and explains how engineers verify complex semiconductor designs before they become physical silicon. Using practical and student-friendly examples, we will walk through the journey from a design specification to test planning, simulation, stimulus generation, checking, coverage, and finally debugging failures. We will also discuss how technologies such as SystemVerilog, UVM, assertions, emulation, and automation help engineers uncover difficult bugs hidden inside increasingly complex SoCs. Thrinadh Dasyam, Bio: Thrinadh Dasyam is a Design Verification Engineer at Intel with more than 21 years of experience in semiconductor design verification and validation. His experience spans ASIC, SoC, and FPGA verification, including System Verilog/UVM, verification planning, functional coverage, emulation, and complex SoC debug and triage. He has also held engineering leadership roles and enjoys mentoring and sharing his industry experience with the next generation of engineers. At UC Berkeley, TD will present "How Do You Find a Bug in a Billion-Transistor Chip?", introducing students to the challenges and techniques behind verifying today's complex semiconductor designs. Christina Schuler, Bio: Christina Delgadillo Schuler brings over a decade of multifaceted experience at Intel Corporation, where she currently serves in Human Resources as a Campus Talent Acquisition based at the Folsom site. Through her 11 years at Intel, Christina has supported Sales & Marketing and Executive Leadership teams before pivoting her expertise to university recruitment. A former collegiate student-athlete, high school and college coach, and educator, Christina brings a uniquely supportive approach to mentoring students, guiding career discovery, and preparing emerging talent for meaningful careers at Intel.

events.title: Welfare Effects of Information Provision on Environmental Externalities | Zac Pond
events.description: Job Market PresentationAbstract Information provision is frequently used to motivate prosocial behavior, yet its impacts on welfare are rarely measured. I study these impacts by combining a signaling model with a series of randomized experiments on personal carbon emissions. The model generates predictions for how information provision can directly affect consumer welfare by altering the relationship between emissions and inferred altruistic type. I implement three interventions, two that provide participants with private information about their emissions and one that publicly reveals them, and measure their welfare effects with an incentive-compatible willingness to pay elicitation. The private information interventions are positive-sum in consumer welfare, whereas public recognition is negative-sum. Nevertheless, 16 to 25 percent of participants pay to avoid receiving private information. Under public recognition, relatively high emitters incur significant utility losses while relatively low emitters receive no gains. I use these estimates to compare the social efficiency of different forms of information provision on externalities.

events.description: Oct 2: Nicholas Isherwood (MORRISON)TITLE: TESSITURA: VOCAL REGISTERSCONCERT: 8pm CNMATBIO: The Franco-American bass Nicholas Isherwood did musical, literary and theatrical studies at Oberlin College (B.A. in French Literature, B.M. in voice with Richard Miller), The Actors Centre in London and the Ecole des Hautes Etudes (D.E.A. in Musicology). An eclectic artist, Isherwood has sung medieval music with Joel Cohen, baroque music with William Christie, the Magic Flute at the Salle Pleyel, Wagner's Meistersinger with Zubin Mehta, several world premieres by Karlheinz Stockhausen and an evening at the Knitting Factory with Steve Lacy. His interest for contemporary music has led him to work with composers such as Sylvano Bussotti, Elliot Carter, George Crumb, Mauricio Kagel, György Kurtág, Olivier Messiaen, Giacinto Scelsi, Karlheinz Stockhausen and Iannis Xenakis as well as the leading composers of younger generations. He has performed both the Bach and Gubaidulina St. John Passions with Helmuth Rilling and improvised with Joëlle Léandre, Steve Lacy, David Moss and Sainkho Namtchilak. Isherwood has sung on five continents, including the greatest theaters in Europe and the United States (Ravinia, Tanglewood, the Disney Hall, La Scala, the Teatro dell'Opera in Rome, Covent Garden, the Châtelet, the Théatre des Champs Elysées, the Philharmonie, the Royal Festival Hall, the Concertgebouw, the Biennale in Munich, all three Berlin opera houses, the Moscow Conservatory, the Konzerthaus in Vienna, the Salzburg Festival, the Aix Festival, etc.) and with world class orchestras and ensembles (London Philharmonic, RAI Orchestra, the Philharmonic Orchestra in Paris, the London Sinfonietta, the SWR Orchestra, the Ensemble Intercontemporain, the Ensemble Modern, the Arditti and Diotima Quartets, etc.) Isherwood has recorded 70 CDs for labels such as Erato, Naxos, NEOS, Stockhausen Verlag and Harmonia Mundi. He has participated in films with Stockhausen, Aperghis and Frize for Arte, the WDR and the INA. In addition to his work as a singer, he has directed contemporary music theatre (SMIO in Orléans, Sons d'Hiver, Parvis St. Jean in Dijon, Teatro Regio in Torino, Stuttgart Opera, Tadashi Suzuki's theatre in Togamura, Deutsche Oper Berlin, etc.) and taught master classes in 5 languages on the French Art Song (USC, UdK), Olivier Messiaen (cnsmd in Paris), baroque singing (Cal State LA) and contemporary singing (Salzburg Mozarteum, ARIAM, UdK in Berlin, Munich Conservatory, Milan Conservatory, etc.), given lectures (Harvard, USC, Penn, Stanford, Berkeley, Freie Universität Berlin, IRCAM, etc.) and composed several pieces for voice (2 commissions from the DRAC and one from Art Zoyd). Nicholas Isherwood has taught at numerous universities in the United States, as well as the Ecole Normale de Musique and the Conservatoire National Supérieur in France, the UdK in Berlin and the Hochschule für Musik in Munich. He has published a book, "The Techniques of Singing" (Bärenreiter, 2013), as well as three peer reviewed articles (LIM, the Journal of Singing, Vox Humana). He is professor of singing at the Conservatoire du Pays de Montbéliard and professor of contemporary singing at the Conservatorio di Santa Cecilia.

events.title: Roundtable: Transportation Opportunities and Priorities for a New California Governor
events.description: ITS Berkeley will present a roundtable discussion in Transportation Opportunities and Priorities for California at 3 p.m. in the Bauer Wurster Hall Auditorium on Oct. 2, 2026.Join the Institute of Transportation Studies for an engaging discussion on the most pressing mobility challenges facing California's next governor. Our panelists will dive into what's working, what needs fixing, and the policies required for the future of transportation.Topicsthe panel will cover include:Solving the transportation funding crisis.How do we get riders back on transit?Enhancing EV market share and the challenges and opportunities of self-driving cars.Linking land use, climate goals, and how much we drive. Moderator: Egon Terplan, Senior Policy Advisor, ITS Berkeley Senior Fellow Panelists: Ken Alex, Director of Project Climate at UC Berkeley Scott Moura, UC Berkeley Civil and Environmental Engineering Professor and Partners for Advanced Transportation Technology Director Susan Shaheen, UC Berkeley Civil and Environmental Engineering Professor and Transportation Sustainability Research Center Director Laura Tolkoff, SPUR Transportation Policy Director Bios:Ken Alex is the Director of Project Climate at the University of California, Berkeley, focusing on the most promising climate solutions and moving them more quickly to policy and scale. From 2011 to 2018, Ken was a Senior Policy Adviser to Governor Jerry Brown, Director of the Governor's Office of Planning and Research, and Chair of the Strategic Growth Council, focusing on climate, energy, environment, and land use issues. Before joining the Governor's Office, Ken was the Senior Assistant Attorney General heading the environment section of the California Attorney General's Office, and the co-head of the Office's global warming unit. From 2000 to 2006, Ken led the California Attorney General's energy task force, investigating price and supply issues related to California's energy crisis. Ken is a graduate of Harvard Law School and holds a B.A. in political theory from the University of California at Santa Cruz. Scott Moura is a Professor in Civil & Environmental Engineering, Director of the Energy, Controls, & Applications Lab (eCAL), and Faculty Director of PATH. He received the B.S. degree from the University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA, and the M.S. and Ph.D. degrees from the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, in 2006, 2008, and 2011, respectively, all in mechanical engineering. From 2011 to 2013, he was a Post-Doctoral Fellow at the Cymer Center for Control Systems and Dynamics, University of California, San Diego and a Visiting Researcher at the Centre Automatique et Systèmes, MINES ParisTech, Paris, France in 2013. His research interests include control, optimization, and AI for batteries, electrified vehicles, and distributed energy resources. Susan Shaheen is a professor in Civil and Environmental Engineering at the University of California, Berkeley. She also co-directs the Transportation Sustainability Research Center of the Institute of Transportation Studies (ITS)-Berkeley and is the director of the UC ITS' Resilient and Innovative Mobility Initiative. Throughout her more than 25-year career, Shaheen has focused on sustainable transportation technologies, environmental/energy policy, behavioral understanding and environmental impacts. She is recognized as a leading international expert in innovative mobility strategies and was among the first to research and write about the changing dynamics in several areas, including shared mobility and autonomy. Her research focuses on electrification and alternative fuels, innovative mobility strategies, behavioral dynamics and public policy as it relates to sustainable transportation and social equity. Shaheen earned a Ph.D. from UC Davis and a M.S. from the University of Rochester. She is a member of the Transportation Research Board's (TRB) Executive Committee – serving as chair in 2021 and vice-chair in 2020 – and the California Transportation Foundation Board since 2022, where she serves as co-chair of the Scholarship Committee. Shaheen received the 2017 Roy W. Crum award from TRB for her distinguished achievements in transportation research. Egon Terplan is CA FWD's Regionalism Fellow. In that role he researches and writes about opportunities to strengthen and improve California's system of regional economic development and planning. He has served as an advisor and consultant to CA FWD since 2022. He is concurrently a Senior Fellow at UC Berkeley's Institute of Transportation Studies where he studies and writes about the future of transit, downtowns, and cities. He continues to maintain a portfolio of external clients focused strategy and policy advisory services. Prior to 2022, Egon was the Senior Advisor for Economic Development and Transportation within the Governor's Office of Planning and Research and the California Strategic Growth Council. In that role he helped launch and manage "Regions Rise Together" a Governor's initiative which resulted in the creation of the Community Economic Resilience Fund (now California Jobs First) and the Regional Early Action Planning Grants 2.0. Egon received a Master of City Planning from UC Berkeley's College of Environmental Design and graduated Phi Beta Kappa from Swarthmore College in Pennsylvania. He has been a visiting professor and lecturer at UC Berkeley, Stanford University, the University of San Francisco, and San Jose State University. From 2021 to 2023 he held the Robert S. Cornish Endowed Chair of Regional Planning and Lecturer in City & Regional Planning at UC Berkeley. Laura Tolkoff is SPUR's transportation policy director. She believes that a sustainable transportation system is the scaffolding for a society that cares for the environment, that embraces public life, and that is healthier, more just, and more prosperous. In addition to overseeing SPUR's transportation portfolio, her areas of focus include public transit, land use integration, project delivery, governance change, and interregional coordination. Laura has worked for SPUR since 2015 in various roles, overseeing several strategic local and regional initiatives and was SPUR's first San José policy director from 2015 to 2017. Prior to joining SPUR, Laura held a senior role managing the energy and environment program at Regional Plan Association (RPA) in the New York Metropolitan area during and after Hurricane Sandy. She spearheaded federal, state, and regional reforms and worked in coalition to launch a federal design competition that brought over $1 billion to local climate resilience projects. Laura earned a Master's degree in urban and environmental policy and planning from Tufts University and a Bachelor's degree in media studies from the University of California at Berkeley. She is an American Leadership Forum senior fellow and was named to Mass Transit magazine's "Top 40 under 40" in 2019.

events.title: Student Probability/PDE Seminar: The KPZ Fixed Point and the Directed Landscape IV
events.description: Speaker: Fraydoun Rezakhanlou, UC BerkeleyThe KPZ equation was proposed in 1986 by Kardar, Parisi and Zhang as a model for stochastic growth interfaces. It is conjectured that many stochastic height functions will converge to KPZ fixed point under 1:2:3 scaling. Simultaneous construction of KPZ fixed points for different initial data yields the directed landscape. In these talks I will give an overview of the existing results for the KPZ fixed points and their associated directed landscape.

events.title: "Anti-Muslim Racism and Genocide" Featuring Prof. Sherene Razack (UCLA)
events.location: 3335 Dwinelle Hall (Level C) University of California Berkeley, CA 94720-2550
events.description: Event Description: This presentation examines anti-Muslim race-making and the question of Palestine; it explore how the figure of the Muslim is transformed into a racial rather than an exclusively religious figure in the colonial imaginary. Speaker bio: Sherene H. Razack is a Distinguished Professor and the Penny Kanner Endowed Chair in the Department of Gender Studies, UCLA. She is an interdisciplinary critical race and feminist scholar whose work engages several fields including Sociology, Legal Studies, Gender Studies, Ethnic Studies, American Studies and Political Science. With a central focus on racial violence, she explores how imperialism, colonialism, capitalism and patriarchy interlock to produce and sustain a racially structured world where racialized populations are marked as disposable and subjected to an unrelenting violence. She is the founder of the Racial Violence Hub, a virtual network of scholars (Racialviolencehub.com). Her books and publications examine settler colonialism, colonialism, neo-colonialism and global white supremacy with a particular focus on the gendered effects of anti-Indigenous, anti-Black, anti-Asian and anti-Muslim racism as they operate in law. Her two most recent books are: Nothing Has to Make Sense: Upholding White Supremacy Through Anti-Muslim Racism (2022) and Dying from Improvement: Inquests and Inquiries into Indigenous Deaths in Custody (2015).

events.title: Materialities of Empire
events.description: Attention to material has become almost ubiquitous in recent architectural history, both extending and revising a modernist tradition of interest in material innovation and expression. Whether through the lens of an ethics of representation, building technology, environmental concerns, supply-chain tracing, the expansion of historical agency to more-than-human beings, or new extensions of the tradition of historical materialism, recent work on architectural materials has both reflected received disciplinary formations and opened up new frameworks and connections. We shift our attention from the materialities of architecture to the materialities of empire in order to bring critical, theoretical, historical, and historiographic questions to the fore in explorations of architecture's material dimensions. Imperialism, after all, was a historical system constructed to exercise control not only over land and people, but also resources and materials. While the histories of building materials are often inseparable from imperial and colonial relations, a gap remains between the study of these two aspects of architecture. Join us for a panel discussion featuring Charmaine Chua (Associate Professor of Geography, UC Berkeley), Liz Galvez, (Assistant Professor of Architecture, UC Berkeley), and Anna Tsing (Professor of Anthropology, UC Santa Cruz) as they explore new approaches to thinking about the relationship between architecture, materiality, and empire. Convened by Irene Cheng (Assistant Professor of Architecture, CCA), James Graham (Assistant Professor of Architecture, CCA), Andrew Herscher (Professor of Architecture, University of Michigan), and Diana Martinez (Assistant Professor of Architecture, UC Berkeley).

events.description: Berkeley World Language Project - 2026-2027 LEARN | CONNECT | INSPIREJoin us for a year of learning in community! Practical Strategies & Real Classroom Impact Engaging Workshops: Practical ideas you can use right away Supportive Community: Collaborate with educators who inspire Student Success: Build world language skills that last Office Hours: Collaborate between workshop sessions! Strand A: Building Lessons for Real World Competence Collaborate, Innovate, Invigorate: Next-level Lessons for every classroom. Invigorate your teaching this year! This strand is for all language teachers who want to take their instruction to the next level, whether beginning or experienced. You will collaborate to develop lessons that focus on teaching in the target language with comprehensible input, guided practice, grammar in context and formative assessment for all levels of proficiency. You will build a complete Lesson over time while learning and practicing strategies to implement immediately. Prerequisite: an open mind, curiosity, and a desire to grow. Strand B: Creating Authentic Themed Units for Today's Learners Develop meaningful, real-life themed Units for modern language learners. Build a thematic unit grounded in authentic materials that reflect real language and culture. You will learn how to design a unit that aligns with UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), AP themes and CA World Languages Standards while integrating global competence, social justice, and social-emotional learning. Using backward design, you'll craft essential questions, Can-Do statements, and assessments that support meaningful communication across all modes—creating immersive, relevant learning experiences that connect students to the real world and help them grow as confident, culturally aware language users. Prerequisite: Strand A or equivalent recommended. events.title: Film Screening: My Undesirable Friends
events.description: At the close of the five-and-a-half-hour film My Undesirable Friends: Part I—Last Air in Moscow, the last remaining holdouts of non-state news media in Russia are driven into exile. Already labeled "foreign agents," harassed, jailed, and sometimes killed, they flee the country within days of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022. This epic, thrillingly urgent sequel, likewise shot on an iPhone, records their fates since. The largely young, female protagonists scatter first to Istanbul, then throughout Europe and beyond. Officially banned at home, stubbornly independent TV Rain persists in reaching millions of Russians from a new headquarters in Latvia, even as constantly shifting politics imperil every refuge. Meanwhile, spies, threats, poisoning, further forced relocations, long-distance liquidation of personal assets, and other bitter pills constitute these brave colleagues' reminders of "home." Nonetheless, they keep reporting truths whose expression could exact the ultimate price, even as other nations (including our own) edge toward crackdowns on the free press.

events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: Film Screening: Band of Outsiders
events.description: Would-be tough guys Franz (Sami Frey) and Arthur (Claude Brasseur) have little better to do than drive around Paris and act out scenes from B movies. But when they team up with Franz's English-class crush, wide-eyed Odile (Anna Karina), to plot a burglary, they stumble into the gap between playacting and reality. Jean-Luc Godard said, "It is not the people who are important, but the atmosphere between them." The atmosphere arises not only from the actors' interplay—their dance in a café and their sprint through the Louvre are among the most memorable and joyous moments in Godard's cinema—but also from Raoul Coutard's exquisitely bleak cinematography and Michel Legrand's jaunty, melancholy score.
