events.title: Art on the Fractured US-Mexico Border | Graduate Work in Progress Lecture by Isa Bratton-Benfield
events.location: Library of French Thought, 4229 Dwinelle Hall
events.description: The US-Mexico border is a site where invasive digital technologies are deployed for surveillance. This is the culmination of decades of expanded funding in surveillance infrastructure. Artists and researchers have critically engaged with this border regime by exposing its systemic failures and interrogating the authoritarian ideological frameworks that underpin it. This lecture presents a guidebook with primary research that details the digital border—an unconstitutional dragnet that violates civil liberties and human rights—and the creative practices that challenge it. Fifth meeting of the graduate work-in-progress series "New Border Imaginaries in an Age of Security." Convened by Professors Debarati Sanyal (French) and Rhiannon Welch (Italian Studies), this interdisciplinary series of graduate student works-in-progress is part of "A Counter-Imaginary in Authoritarian Times," a joint project of the Center for Interdisciplinary Critical Inquiry and the International Consortium of Critical Theory Programs that develops strategies to counteract new forms of authoritarianism.Isa Bratton-Benfield is a PhD student in the Film & Media Department at UC Berkeley. Her research documents the design of physical data infrastructures, their genealogies, questions of data sovereignty, and their geopolitical valences. She has published work in the Sourcing Journal, Journal of Visual Culture, and has a forthcoming publication in Oxford Intersections: Borders. Before coming to UC Berkeley, Isa worked at the Cornell Global Labor Institute and Maharam, and received her MSc in Media, Communication, and Development from the London School of Economics & Political Science.

events.title: (Screening) No Monastery, No Village | Voices from the Roof of the World
events.description: HELP NEPAL Organizations Accepting Flood-Relief Donations In recognition of the devastating mud flood that struck Nepal's Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems on August 26, claiming thousands of lives, ISAS will screen a documentary about a remote Himalayan village (located in Limi Valley of Humla District, northwestern Nepal) with an eleventh-century Buddhist monastery at its center confronting the threat of a catastrophic glacial flood. Produced in 2024, the documentary examines the accelerating effects of climate change on Himalayan glaciers and the resulting dangers of glacial erosion, instability, and flooding. It therefore offers a timely perspective on the environmental conditions underlying the recent tragic flooding. Directed by climate activist and filmmaker Tashi Lhazom (https://nepalclimatehub.org/climate-champions/thasi-lhazom), the film is part of the series Voices from the Roof of the World (https://www.aku.edu/vrw/Pages/home.aspx), produced by Aga Khan University in collaboration with Shanta Nepali Productions.Running time: 28 minutes. Watch the trailer HERE (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wDBhThOUHjk). The screening will be followed by a panel discussion with:Tashi Lhazom (https://nepalclimatehub.org/climate-champions/thasi-lhazom), Film Director (joining remotely)Ramesh Bhushal (https://earthjournalism.net/who-we-are/staff/ramesh-bhushal), Nepal-based environmental journalist, writer, and documentary reporter (joining remotely)Ran Ran (https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=oSdIhKQAAAAJ&hl=en) 冉冉, Senior Research Fellow at the School of Government, Shenzhen University and currently based in Stanford Matthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer), Assistant Professor of History, UC Berkeley. The discussion will be moderated by Alexander von Rospatt (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/alexander-von-rospatt), Professor of Buddhist and South Asian Studies and Director of the Group in Buddhist Studies at UC Berkeley.Hybrid Event: Attend in person or online via Zoom. Online attendees must register for Zoom (https://berkeley.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_avDi1InTQXCrNjCAA9SkjQ); there will be no Facebook livestream. ————–DATE: Wed, October 7, 2026 TIME: 5:30-7 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall NOTE: Attend in person or online via Zoom. Online attendees must register for Zoom (https://berkeley.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_avDi1InTQXCrNjCAA9SkjQ); there will be no Facebook livestream. —————- ABOUT THE DOCUMENTARY High in Nepal's remote Limi Valley, the village of Halzi is home to around 500 people whose lives revolve around the 11th-century Waltse Rinchenling Buddhist Monastery, the spiritual and cultural heart of the community. But just a few kilometers upstream, a rapidly melting glacier poses an existential threat. A previous glacial flood has already caused destruction, and scientists warn that another could wipe out both the village and the monastery. The film follows residents as they confront an impossible choice: leave their ancestral home for safety, or remain to protect a sacred way of life rooted in faith, memory, and place. Through the experiences of villagers including monk Sonam Dhondup and yak herder Pema Dolma, the documentary explores the tension between devotion and survival, revealing how climate change is not only transforming a Himalayan landscape but also threatening an entire cultural world. Running time 28 minutes. See the trailer HERE (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wDBhThOUHjk) ABOUT THE DIRECTORTashi Lhazom (https://nepalclimatehub.org/climate-champions/thasi-lhazom) is a prominent youth climate advocate working at the intersection of climate action, gender equality, indigenous rights, and political and climate literacy. She has spoken at grassroots, national, and global platforms, and is a co-founder of two civil society initiatives. With the wide range of hats that Tashi wears, she is also a filmmaker that harnesses the power of storytelling to promote generational change in delivering climate justice. "No Monastery, No Village" is her directorial debut based on the nexus of climate change and cultural heritage of indigenous people. As an academician, she covers climate diplomacy and politics. She holds an undergraduate degree from Hindu College, University of Delhi. She specializes in Climate Politics. ABOUT THE PANELISTS Dr. Ran Ran (https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=oSdIhKQAAAAJ&hl=en) 冉冉 is a Senior Research Fellow at the School of Government, Shenzhen University. Her research interests include comparative environmental politics, climate change and climate justice. Prior to joining Shenzhen University, Dr. Ran was an Associate Professor at Renmin University of China. She earned her Ph.D. from the University of Duisburg-Essen in 2009 and subsequently held a postdoctoral fellowship at the University of Southern California from 2009 to 2010. Dr. Ran's research has been published in journals including the Journal of Environmental Policy & Planning, The China Quarterly, and the Journal of Cleaner Production, among others. Her current book project examines how strong state capacity in authoritarian systems produces both effective environmental outcomes, blame politics and environmental injustice, particularly for vulnerable rural communities. Her 2015 book examined the paradox of the "environmental policy implementation gap" in China's local authoritarian environmentalism. Dr. Ran was selected as one of the "Chinese Highly Cited Researchers in Political Science" by Elsevier from 2021 to 2025.Ramesh Bhushal (https://earthjournalism.net/who-we-are/staff/ramesh-bhushal) isRamesh Bhushal is an award-winning environmental journalist and writer based in Kathmandu, Nepal. With nearly two decades of reporting, his work focuses on climate change, rivers, biodiversity loss, and transboundary water issues across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region. He currently works as the South Asia Coordinator for the Earth Journalism Network, a global network of environmental journalists. Bhushal has reported for major international and regional outlets, including the BBC Nepali, The Guardian, Dialogue Earth, The Associated Press, and The Himalayan Times. In 2024, he published his acclaimed debut travelogue, Chhalbato: Kailash dekhi Ganga samma (Down the Demon River: A Journey from Kailash to the Ganga), which documents a 2,000-kilometer expedition following the Karnali River basin across Tibet, Nepal, and India. The book earned him Nepal's prestigious Padmashree Literature Award in 2025. A recipient of the 2010 WWF Nepal Media in Conservation Award, Bhushal holds a master's degree in environmental science and advocates for slow, field-based journalism. His work can be read at www.himalayaspeaks.com (https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.himalayaspeaks.com?utm_source%3Dgemini&source=gmail-imap&ust=1791118881000000&usg=AOvVaw0sAUMDad24uJeIPPUOlr97)Matthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer) is Assistant Professor of History at University of California, Berkeley. He is an environmental historian of South Asia. His research and teaching focus on the place of the environment in global history, with particular attention to fossil fuels, agriculture, forests, climate change, and environmental politics. His work also connects global environmental history to histories of law, capitalism, post-colonial development, the earth sciences, and photography. He is the author of Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis. EVENT POSTER —————— Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. events.title: Tang Music in Contemporary China: Sensing Artistry Through Time
events.description: Tang Music in Contemporary China: Sensing Artistry Through Time October 8 Keynote Lecture (125 Morrison Hall) October 9 (125 Morrison Hall) October 10 (Hertz Hall)— Full program available here (https://events.berkeley.edu/live/files/61-music-program) — The resplendent court-entertainment music of the Tang dynasty (618–907 CE), born from cultural exchange along the early Silk Road, has always loomed large in histories of Chinese music. But in today's China, reconstructive performances of this music have begun to assert its place — as living, breathing performance art — in concert halls and social media feeds, too. This conference brings together scholars and performers from across the world, including leading and emerging experts from China, to present, evaluate, and propel forward global scholarly and artistic discourse on Tang music in the contemporary world. Papers will explore the material culture of the Silk Road, early notations and musical instruments, techniques of historical reconstruction and performance, and the place of historical music and dance in contemporary Chinese society. Three leading ensembles from China and the United States will give live performances of Tang music and dance, followed by a roundtable discussion bringing scholarship and performance into critical dialogue.

events.title: Author Larissa Lai: Echolocating Asian Canadian Studies: A Poethical Method for the Long COVID Moment
events.description: At the height of the COVID pandemic, the bat emerged from the Wuhan wet market as a racializing figure entangled with tropes of infection and consumption, re-activating late 19th century associations of Asians with disease. This essay reclaims the bat, both as a figure and as an existing animal, to consider how to engage with Asian Canadian Studies in this historical moment. Both racial and state formations are impossible to claim in essentializing or nationalist ways, and yet, "Asian Canadian" remains a productive location from which to do the work of both community building and critique. This talk considers phenomenological and poethical approaches to cultural embodiment, with a particular focus on the bat's ability to orient itself in flight by echolocation. Echolocation can be used to consider three possible moments of inception for Asian Canadian Studies - the 1910s, the 1970s, and the 1990s. It can also be used to consider the field's relationships with Indigenous Studies, Black Canadian Studies, Asian American Studies, and Queer and Gender Studies.Larissa Lai is the author of nine books including The Lost Century, The Tiger Flu, Salt Fish Girl, and Slanting I, Imagining We: Asian Canadian Literary Production in the 1980s and 1990s. Recipient of the Jim Duggins Novelist's Prize, the Lambda Literary Award, the Astraea Award, and the Otherwise Honor Book, she has also been a finalist for the ACQL Gabrielle Roy Prize for Literary Criticism, the Books in Canada First Novel Award and the Governor General's Award. She is currently the Richard Charles Lee Chair of Chinese Canadian Studies at the University of Toronto. Born in California, Professor Lai grew up in Newfoundland. She received her BA from the University of British Columbia, her MA from the University of East Anglia, and her PhD from the University of Calgary.

events.title: Cycads, Wild Black Peppers, and Amazonian roots: the role of plant specialized chemistry at three different scales
events.description: Specialized metabolites play critical roles in plant evolution and ecology, yet most of what we know about this rich and diverse organic arsenal comes from foliar tissues and local scales. As chemical ecology is being transformed by higher-resolution instrumentation and novel machine-learning approaches for data processing and analysis, scientists have ventured into larger-scale studies (geographically, environmentally, and phylogenetically). Furthermore, a more "holistic" understanding of plant chemistry has highlighted key differences in the likely mechanisms driving the evolution of chemical diversity across plant tissues. In this talk, I will present three research projects that highlight the role of plant specialized metabolites across different scales (from local to regional). This project also highlights fundamental trade-offs and constraints on phytochemical arsenals across plant tissues (leaves, roots, and seeds).

events.title: Seminar 242, Econometrics Seminar: Grigory Franguridi (University of Southern California) - Robust estimation and inference with given marginals
events.description: Abstract: We consider two-step estimation of a finite-dimensional target parameter, where the first step is the nonparametric estimation of a joint density given known marginals, and the second step is the moment estimation of the target parameter. We derive the influence function for this estimation procedure and show that it depends on a nonparametric additive regression. We explain how to compute the influence function using a version of the extensively studied smooth backfitting algorithm. This leads to a Neyman-orthogonal (debiased) estimator for the target parameter and a procedure for asymptotically valid inference. We consider two applications of our results in detail: a panel data model with (nonparametric) nonignorable attrition and refreshment samples (Hirano et al., 2001) and the optimal transport with entropic regularization (Cuturi, 2013; Galichon and Salanié, 2022). We show in Monte Carlo simulations that our estimator indeed reduced bias, and the associated confidence intervals exhibit coverage close to nominal.

events.title: Shing-Tung Yau and Yu-Yun Yau Endowed Lecture in Mathematics, dedicated to Shoshichi Kobayashi: Fully local Chern–Simons theories
events.description: Speaker: Dan Freed, Harvard UniversityAbstract: It has long been a challenge to construct fully local extensions of 3-dimensional topological Chern–Simons theories. The problem appears in various forms: "Extend Chern–Simons down to points" or "What does Chern–Simons theory attach to a point?". In recent work with Claudia Scheimbauer and Constantin Teleman, we apply the cobordism hypothesis to realize fully local extensions of Reshetikhin–Turaev theories, which include Chern–Simons theories. I will give an overview of the problem before getting on to the new work.

events.title: Symposium on Trans Negativity
events.location: 315 Wheeler Hall (Maude Fife Room), UC Berkeley, and The Lab, 2948 16th St, San Francisco
events.description: Trans negativity names a negative relation to trans life, as it presents itself in the devaluation of trans people across contemporary discourses, the withholding of rights and care, and the mobilization of suffering in public policy and anti-gender movements. At the same time, trans negativity also names an exciting turn within trans thought that, drawing on debates that have shaped queer theory for over two decades, refuses to be edifying and instead embraces the bleak, dissociative, and antagonistic. This symposium seeks to engage various senses of the negative and to elaborate its implications for trans study. Gathering scholars and artists working across psychoanalysis, aesthetics, theory, and political history, our program takes on negativity as an occasion for collective thought and practice.Program:Thursday, October 8, 4 - 5:30 pm Maude Fife, 315 Wheeler Hall, UC Berkeley. Grace Lavery presents her new book Personal Demons, in conversation with Jessy Nyiri and Ava Kim.Friday, October 9,9.45am - 6 pm Maude Fife, 315 Wheeler Hall, UC Berkeley. events.title: 2026 Gerald D. Feldman Lecture | Reckoning with the Past in Germany and the United States: The Case for Thinking Comparatively about Reparative Justice
events.description: German atonement for the Holocaust has been widely hailed by the international community as a paragon of national reckoning, and over the last decade, African American intellectuals such as Ta-Nehisi Coates have explicitly invoked Germany as a useful model in their calls for Americans to confront the legacy of slavery and other forms of state-sanctioned racism. In this lecture, Rita Chin, will trace the complicated, fraught 80-year process by which Germans have dealt with the Nazi past, focusing on developments and debates in the Federal Republic. She will consider the specific ways in which the German case is instructive for Americans seeking to pursue redress but also explore how Germany's vaunted memory culture has become fossilized such that it has sometimes become a stumbling block for a German society struggling to respond to contemporary challenges. Thinking comparatively about how to reckon with legacies of state-sanctioned racial harm, oppression, and violence not only presents Americans with a concrete template for imagining what reparative justice might look like, Chin suggests, it may also help Germans acknowledge the shape-shifting aspects of racism and perhaps even rethink some of the outdated aspects of their memory culture. Rita Chin, Louise A. Tilly Collegiate Professor of European History and Associate Dean of Social Sciences of the Rackham Graduate School at the University of Michigan, is a historian of modern Europe with particular expertise in immigration and human mobility, race and ethnicity, and colonialism and post-colonialism. Trained in European cultural and intellectual history, she has sought to apply these modes of inquiry to her ongoing interest in how difference and diversity have shaped the very terms of modern Germany and Europe more generally. Her research and writing have been supported by the SSRC, the Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars, the ACLS Burkhardt Fellowship for Recently Tenured Scholars, the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, and the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation. If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: In the Shadow of Genocide: Female Perpetrators of the Armenian Genocide
events.description: Abstract Women are often imagined as victims of war and genocide rather than participants in violence. Yet the genocides of the twentieth century challenged this assumption, revealing that women could also play important roles in persecution and mass killing. This talk explores a largely overlooked aspect of the Armenian Genocide: the involvement of Turkish women in violence against Armenians. Drawing on Armenian survivors' testimonies and memoirs, alongside other historical sources, it examines the many ways women participated—from spreading hatred and encouraging violence to looting, abduction, and, in some cases, direct killing. The evidence also points to forms of organized and institutional involvement that deserve further investigation. By bringing women perpetrators into the story, this talk offers a more complete understanding of how genocide is carried out. It also invites us to rethink common assumptions about gender, violence, and responsibility during one of the twentieth century's defining atrocities.Speaker's BioDr. Edita Gzoyan is a lecturer at the American University of Armenia and Editor-in-Chief of the International Journal of Armenian Genocide Studies. She holds a PhD in International Relations from Yerevan State University and an LL.M. from the American University of Armenia. Her research focuses on the history and legal dimensions of the Armenian Genocide, humanitarian responses and refugee assistance, gender-based violence, forced child transfer, and the post-genocide recovery of Armenian women and children.

events.title: Matthew Shutzer | Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis
events.description: A talk by Matthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer), Assistant Professor of History, on his new book, Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis (https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691265919/until-the-last-ton?srsltid=AfmBOorxSc-xwrFM8YrmGZbYMJ4vEm3ZcucGahHadYBaRZA9ySGhXWds), a panoramic historical account of India's ascent in the global fossil economy. Event moderated by Sharad Chari (https://geography.berkeley.edu/professor-sharad-chari), Associate Professor of Geography, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, Oct 8, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————–About the Book: India is today one of the world's largest producers and consumers of fossil fuels, driving new investments in the global fossil economy and achieving record-breaking levels of coal extraction at home. As the planet burns from climate change, this entrenchment of fossil fuel dependence has left many searching for how we arrived at this point. Until the Last Ton provides a sweeping new appraisal of this planetary dilemma, uncovering how India became part of an emerging fossil capitalism that continues to shape the present. Matthew Shutzer recasts the origins of the fossil economy by showing how European industrialization unleashed a global search for fossil energy in the colonial world. Placing India at the center of this history, Shutzer traces how the highland forests of eastern India became early frontiers for global coal investment, transforming this landscape into the largest site of imperial overseas coal production across a century of colonial rule. At the heart of these shifts was a legal framework of subterranean property, which redefined local relations of land ownership and social power, while tying the growth of India's fossil economy to the progressive ecological destruction of the forest frontier. Following these dynamics into the postcolonial period, Until the Last Ton reveals the enduring impacts of colonial property on independent India's energy history, shedding new light on postwar struggles for energy development and resource sovereignty, as well as the violent conflicts over mining dispossession that have haunted India's economic ascent in an age of climate crisis.About the Author:Matthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer) is Assistant Professor of History at University of California, Berkeley. He is an environmental historian of South Asia. His research and teaching focus on the place of the environment in global history, with particular attention to fossil fuels, agriculture, forests, climate change, and environmental politics. His work also connects global environmental history to histories of law, capitalism, post-colonial development, the earth sciences, and photography. His book, Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis, is the first history of fossil fuels in colonial and post-colonial South Asia. It traces India's rise as a world-leading fossil economy in the twentieth century and examines the processes of empire, capitalism, and agroecological change that shaped this transformation. The book moves beyond the prevailing focus in the environmental history of energy on production and consumption, offering instead a longer-term perspective on land, subsurface property rights, geological knowledge, and mining conflicts. In doing so, it reveals the central role of agrarian development in shaping India's trajectory of fossil fuel dependence. Shutzer is currently working on a second book project examining climate change and the making of the Third World after 1945. Before joining the History Department at UC Berkeley, Shutzer taught as an Assistant Professor in the Department of History at Duke University. He previously served as a Junior Scholar at the Harvard Academy for International and Area Studies at Harvard University and as an S.V. Ciriacy-Wantrup Fellow in Natural Resource Economics and Political Economy in the Department of Geography at UC Berkeley. He has also worked as a researcher on several projects related to the implementation of India's Forest Rights Act in western Odisha. Along with Rebecca Herman, Rebecca McLennan, and Bernadette Perez, Shutzer is one of the faculty conveners of the Berkeley Workshop on Environmental History, based in UC Berkeley's Department of History. events.title: The Significance of Postcolonial Fascism in Cold War Korea
events.location: Institute of East Asian Studies, Conference Room, 2111 Bancroft Way, 5th Floor, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker: Sungik Yang (Arizona State University) Hybrid Event | RSVP/Registration Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Register for Virtual Attendance - COMING SOON Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: The years after Korea's independence from Japanese colonial rule in 1945 were a time of extreme crisis that opened a space for fascist ideologies and discourses to gain ascendancy. In response to national division and political polarization and violence, there arose a heavily nationalist ruling discourse that openly promoted the supremacy of the homogeneous ethnic nation above all competing forms of identity while rejecting core tenets of Western liberalism, containing strong parallels with fascist ideologies in Europe and Japan. Furthermore, this hegemonic discourse pervaded Korean political culture for decades, helping to prop up authoritarian regimes in the country until the 1980s. This discourse, which I call "transcendent nationalism," was a product of the intersection of Korea's postcolonial and Cold War conditions. It sought to overcome Cold War divisions through an embrace of the Korean nation while maintaining colonial-era suspicions of Western capitalist modernity. Ultimately, the fascistic aspects of South Korea's post-1945 political culture reveals the liminal position that Koreans found themselves in during the Cold War, being pulled into the U.S.'s anticommunist orbit but expressing discomfort with American political and cultural hegemony. In addition, postcolonial Korea emerges as an intriguing case study to better understand the nature of fascism as a political discourse promoting an alternative form of modernity that rejected those of capitalist liberalism and communism. By analyzing how fascism took root in a postcolonial nation-state after World War II, we can also gain an understanding of fascism's enduring appeal in global politics even today. Speaker Bio: Sungik Yang is an assistant professor of history at Arizona State University. He is a political and intellectual historian of modern Korea, focusing on political ideology, nationalism, democracy, and historical memory. His forthcoming book is titled Nation Transcendent: Postcolonial Fascism in Cold War Korea.

events.title: Wrinkles in time: Inquiries into aging, historicity, and generational meaning
events.description: In this talk David Divita brings together three projects that seem unrelated but nevertheless share a commitment to understanding the temporal complexities of everyday discourse. He begin by discussing the ethnographic research on Spaniards in later life that he conducted as a Ph.D. student in RLL (French), tracing its slow evolution into a book manuscript about how silence can operate as a generative form of communication. He then turns to his ongoing case study of the Valley of Cuelgamuros, a fascist memorial complex outside of Madrid that has long been the focal point of heated debates about the possibilities and limitations of monumental resignification. Lastly, Divita goes on to feature his current project, From plague to PrEP: Gay Gen X and the meaning of midlife, for which he did 50 in-depth interviews with gay men from around the United States who were born between 1965 and 1980. These members of so-called Generation X were not as directly impacted by the AIDS crisis as their forebears, but their coming-of-age was nevertheless marked by a sense of danger and mortality well into the 1990s, when retroviral treatments first became available. He highlights some of the themes that have emerged in his analysis of these data – such as the rejection of chrononormativity and the prevalence of non-monogamy – proposing "gay man" as a generational type. Throughout the talk, Divita underscore the methods, concepts, and questions from linguistic anthropology that have shaped his thinking across projects. He also integrates personal reflections to illuminate the decisions and detours that comprise his intellectual trajectory.David Divita is a professor of Romance Languages at Pomona College, whose research is grounded in linguistic anthropology and sociocultural linguistics. His book, Untold stories: Legacies of authoritarianism among Spanish labour migrants in later life, was published by University of Toronto Press in 2024. The following year it was translated into Spanish and published by Postmetropolis Editorial (Madrid). Prof. Divita has published articles in Journal of Linguistic Anthropology, Language in Society, Journal of Sociolinguistics, History and Anthropology, Discourse & Society, and Journal of Language, Culture and Society, among others. He received his Ph.D. in Romance Languages, with a specialization in French and Spanish linguistics, from UC Berkeley in 2010.

events.title: Film Screening: Union Town
events.description: Two-time Best Documentary Feature Academy Award winner Barbara Kopple nabbed her first in 1976 for Harlan County, USA, which chronicled Kentucky coal miners' bitter but ultimately successful strike for better working conditions. American Dream(1990) was less upbeat: Threatened with pay cuts or no jobs at all, Minnesota meatpacking plant workers found a decade of Reaganomics had thoroughly weakened their bargaining power. Decades later, the director's focus is a whole new labor sector as she completes the trilogy she began fifty years ago. Those who serve UPS, Amazon, and apps like Door Dash deliver 2.4 million packages every day within New York City alone. Many aren't official employees, but rather third-party contractors sans benefits or job protection, their toil frequently underpaid, exhausting, and sometimes downright dangerous. Meanwhile, the corporations themselves make astronomical profits. Can unions, activism, and strikes still secure livable wages, among other basic needs that are rapidly disappearing for many in the twenty-first century? Full of real-life drama and compelling personalities, Kopple's latest is a true sign of our times.

events.title: BETR/EECS Solid State Technologies Seminar: Dr. Thaddeus Ladd, HRL Laboratories | A Digitally Controlled Silicon Quantum Processing Unit
events.description: Abstract: Commercially relevant quantum computers will require large numbers of high-performing qubits that can be manufactured, integrated and controlled at scale. Silicon exchange-only qubits are a strong candidate modality owing to their control-signal simplicity and compatibility with advanced semiconductor manufacturing, but questions remain around the achievability of sufficiently low noise and a scalable control and wiring solution. We introduce a quantum processing unit composed of a custom-designed cryogenic complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) controller, a high-density superconducting ribbon cable and a low-noise exchange-only qubit device. The quantum chip features a 3-rail array of 54 exchange-coupled quantum dots, configurable to host up to 18 exchange-only qubits. We integrate and use these components to demonstrate qubit performance for both single-qubit and entangling operations that advances the exchange-only state of the art by an order of magnitude. We further validate this system by implementing a distance-5 repetition code and a distance-2 quantum error-detecting code and then make detailed comparisons with simulations. Our work facilitates the development of future utility-scale quantum computers with manageable operational and capital requirements. Bio: Dr. Thaddeus Ladd is presently Chief Scientist of the Computational Physics Division of HRL Laboratories, an IBM company. His key focus in this role is the development of silicon spin qubits and their viability for future quantum computers, but he also contributes efforts to improve quantum sensors and quantum communication systems. Thaddeus has been in the field of quantum computing for over a quarter century now, starting straight after receiving his bachelor's in physics from Harvey Mudd College in 1998. He received a Masters and Ph.D. in applied physics from Stanford University as a Hertz fellow, graduating in 2005. Thaddeus continued research at Stanford, via project researcher roles with the University of Tokyo and Japan's National Institute of Informatics, prior to starting at HRL in 2009.

events.title: BLC Talk | Toward Principled AI Use: Co-Creating Multiliteracies-Oriented L2 Materials with Generative AI | Dr. Kristen Michelson
events.description: Toward Principled AI Use: Co-Creating Multiliteracies-Oriented L2 Materials with Generative AI Dr. Kristen Michelson Associate Professor, Applied Linguistics and French, Texas Tech University The rapid release of openly accessible generative AI chatbots and other apps has created a plethora of new opportunities in world language (WL) education. While generative-AI tools can create efficiencies in our workflows as teachers, they also have the potential to constrain innovation, as AI tools do not create, but rather generate text from patterns in training data. By their very nature, they are reflective of past practices and discourses. This calls for principled, judicious use of AI tools in developing materials for WL education. Taking specific cases of AI-generated teaching and assessment materials, I will demonstrate how zero-shot prompts to AI chatbots perpetuate the status quo in WL education, and constrain possibilities for innovation. However, when approached with rigorously defined disciplinary concepts (Cope & Kalantzis, 2023), AI tools can be beneficial collaborators. Drawing on key tenets of multiliteracies pedagogies and ACTFL World Readiness Standards, I will show how AI can be used productively by WL teachers as co-participants in materials creation. First, we will collaboratively analyze sample AI-generated assessments, texts, and rubrics. Next, we will examine multiliteracies core practices and re-analyze these materials in that light. Finally, we will look at specific prompts and discuss ways AI can be used to help instructors design and implement literacy-oriented WL materials. Reference Cope, B., & Kalantzis, M. (2023). A multimodal grammar of artificial intelligence: Measuring the gains and losses in generative AI(link is external). Multimodality & Society, 4(2), 123-152. Bio: Kristen Michelson is Associate Professor in Applied Linguistics and French at Texas Tech University, where she directs the first- and second-year French language program. Her research centers on multiliteracies pedagogies, and aims to promote paradigm change in L2 teaching and learning toward approaches that foreground culture, affect, identities, and ideological discourses. Recent work includes examining L2 learners' multimodal reading processes, developing core practices for multiliteracies pedagogies, and exploring implications of generative AI for L2 literacies and materials development. Dr. Michelson has led numerous workshops for language teachers worldwide, inviting participants to reflect on biases and beliefs through collaborative, discovery-oriented activities.

events.title: Film Screening: When a Witness Recants
events.description: With her trademark command of complex social issues and deeply human storytelling, veteran documentarian Dawn Porter (John Lewis: Good Trouble) examines the Harlem Park Three—teenagers wrongfully sentenced to life in prison for the 1983 murder of a Baltimore middle schooler. Inspired by Jennifer Gonnerman's New Yorker reporting, the investigative documentary tracks how police coerced thirteen- and fourteen-year-old witnesses into fabricating testimony, and how the state's case collapsed thirty-six years later, in 2019, when those same witnesses formally recanted. Interweaving archival footage, graphic novel–style animation, and tense legal depositions, the film moves past the courtroom to capture the profound emotional toll on the trio, boys who became men behind bars, separated from their families and the world outside. Exploring the possibility of reconciliation between the exonerated and a key childhood witness, Porter ultimately asks what justice, accountability, and healing can look like in the wake of America's longest combined wrongful conviction.

events.title: Glenn T. Seaborg Memorial Lectures in Inorganic Chemistry
events.description: Erwin Reisner, Professor of Energy and Sustainability, University of CambridgeSolar Chemical TechnologiesInspired by the blueprint of photosynthesis, creating synthetic systems for the direct conversion of sunlight into sustainable fuels has long been a defining ambition of chemistry. While decades of research have been spent on developing solar water splitting catalysts to produce green hydrogen, recently a new generation of photosynthesis-inspired architectures capable of directly converting sunlight, carbon dioxide and carbon waste streams has emerged. This advance has been made possible by developing and integrating metal complex and biological catalysts with semiconductor materials and electrodes, together with the engineering of bespoke devices. This lecture will first introduce functional mimics of photosynthesis, which couple semiconductor light absorbers with immobilised (bio)catalysts to achieve solar-driven carbon dioxide fixation alongside water oxidation to oxygen. Next, an alternative strategy will be presented that replaces the challenging water oxidation reaction by the oxidation of waste biomass and plastics. This concept, termed solar reforming, simultaneously improves reaction thermodynamics, enhances overall rate of catalysis, and creates economic value through oxidative valorisation while simultaneously generating clean fuel. The ongoing demonstration of outdoor solar plastic reforming at the kilogram and square-metre scale illustrates the growing potential of this approach as a practical route towards circular solar-powered manufacturing. The lecture will close by giving an overview of emerging frontiers in integrated solar chemistry, including atmospheric CO₂ utilisation, advanced light-management strategies, and solar-powered cascade catalysis for selective chemical organic synthesis. Together, this presentation aims to provide a compelling vision for a new generation of solar technologies that combine carbon capture, plastic and biomass waste valorisation, and renewable chemical manufacturing in integrated, scalable systems. More information: https://www-reisner.ch.cam.ac.uk/

events.title: "Did the Humanities Die in Gaza?" PAS Conference Keynote Address
events.description: This talk will examine the reality of the ongoing genocide unfolding in Gaza, with special reference to the destruction, death, and dispossession experienced by Palestinian universities, academics, and students. Amidst this stark reality, it will discuss the remarkable scholarly struggle to keep the flame of knowledge alive, and the special role that the humanities have played in maintaining the Palestinian tradition of resilient summud. Concurrently, it will probe the ethical, intellectual, social and political implications of the Western humanities establishment's failure to heed our Palestinian colleagues' call for support, and their suppression of any attempt at solidarity. This, it will be argued, is reflective of an existential crisis in our fields that threatens the future of the humanities and, indeed, our very conception of humanity.Speaker bio: Abdel Razzaq Takriti is the Associate Professor of History and Arab-American Educational Foundation Chair in Arab Studies at Rice University. He is the author of Monsoon Revolution: Republicans, Sultans, and Empires in Oman, 1965-1976 (Oxford University Press, 2013). Professor Takriti is also the co-author (with Karma Nabulsi) of the digital humanities project The Palestinian Revolution. He has published extensively in a range of edited volumes and major scholarly journals including The American Historical Review and Radical History Review. Professor Takriti received his doctorate from St Antony's College, University of Oxford. He was the Founding Director of the Arab-American Educational Foundation Center for Arab Studies at the University of Houston, and served in 2022/2023 as the Mahmoud Darwish Visiting Chair in Palestinian Studies at Brown University. He previously taught at the University of Oxford and the University of Sheffield in the UK.

events.title: Film Screening: Elephants in the Fog
events.description: In a village in southern Nepal, Pirati is the matriarch of a Kinnar community, a third-gender tradition recognized in that country, where families form through chosen bonds of care rather than blood. When Apsara, one of Pirati's daughters, disappears during a nightly patrol to keep watch for wild elephants, Pirati begins her own search. As the mystery opens wounds within the community, she wrestles with a difficult choice: remain with the family that gave her a home or pursue a new life with the man she loves. Around them, wild elephants move through the darkness, revered and feared, a haunting presence that echoes the film's questions about belonging and otherness. Abinash Bikram Shah's remarkable first feature is both a tense, immersive thriller and a tender portrait of chosen family, finding beauty in ritual, humor, desire, and everyday life. Noé Bach's stunning cinematography makes the forest feel almost alive, while Frederic Alvarez's haunting score draws us deeper into Pirati's journey. Winner of the Un Certain Regard Jury Prize at the Cannes Film Festival, Elephants in the Fog announces a filmmaker with a remarkably assured vision.

events.title: Film Screening: Sad Girlz
events.description: Fernanda Tovar, in her narrative debut feature—winner of the Crystal Bear for Best Film in Generation 14plus at the Berlinale—crafts a moving coming-of-age drama about friendship, teenage girlhood, and trauma. Rocio Guzmán gives a standout performance as La Maestra, scraping by as best she can to understand how to be a good ally to her friend Paula (Darana Álvarez). Friends and swimmers Paula and La Maestra navigate life with the same confidence they show in the pool. Dreams cast a quiet spell over the early stretches of the film, though its premonitory title, Sad Girlz, suggests that the girls' carefree world will not remain untouched. One night when they go to a party, something happens to Paula. As their journey deepens and complicates their bond, these two remarkable young women provide a sense of warmth that makes Sad Girlz linger in the heart long after the credits roll.

events.title: Film Screening: Minotaur
events.description: The year is 2022 and the backdrop is Vladimir Putin's corruption-drenched Russia in Academy Award nominee Andrey Zvyagintsev's latest, his first feature since 2017's astounding Loveless. A bone-chilling reimagining of both Claude Chabrol's La femme infidèle and Adrian Lyne's Unfaithful, Zvyagintsev's thriller follows the essentials of the source material: Amid various work pressures, a powerful businessman (Dmitriy Mazurov) learns that his increasingly distant wife (Iris Lebedeva) is cheating on him. But the filmmaker also puts a masterfully nihilistic spin on the story's machinations, questioning, with his ingenious inquisitiveness and observantly still camerawork, whether any authority in his motherland would care about unspeakable acts of crime when the country is at war with Ukraine and a sense of lawlessness has seized the higher-ups. The winner of the Grand Prix at the Cannes Film Festival, Minotaur gifts us a parting note that feels like a silent scream with echoes that inhabit the soul.

events.title: Film Screening: On Behalf of My Son
events.description: What does it mean to apologize for something you cannot undo? Gabriel Martins's drama follows a seventy-five-year-old mother after the death of her son, a bus driver whose final journey leaves dozens of lives shattered. Vicentina begins visiting the families of the victims, carrying an apology that may be impossible to accept. But as she moves from one family to another, a more difficult question emerges: Can an apology meant to ease one person's pain ever belong to someone else? Rejane Faria gives one of the year's most empathetic performances, finding extraordinary humanity in Vicentina's silences, hesitations, and small gestures. A native of Contagem in the Brazilian state of Minas Gerais, Martins brings the texture of his home region to a story that could happen anywhere. Delicate, searching, and quietly moving, On Behalf of My Son moves between laughter and tears, leaving us with questions about grief, responsibility, forgiveness, and what it means to live with what cannot be changed.

events.title: Exploration of Forms: Divergent Rhythms with Alexis Riley
events.description: About Exploration of Forms: Exploration of Forms is a public workshop series that centers embodiment, transformation, and creativity. All workshops are free for students. Guests are encouraged to make a donation of $5–20 at the door, but no one will be turned away for lack of funds.Signups are available here: https://tdps.link/explorationAbout This Workshop: This workshop offers an introduction to repetition as a disability cultural movement practice. Inspired by (though in no way mimicking) stimming and guided by an autistic artist, this 90-minute session explores iterative motion as an entry point into somatic exploration and movement improvisation.Everyone is welcome, including autistic/neurodivergent, mad/mentally ill, and disabled people, as well as others who are interested in respectfully engaging disability performance lineages in an accessible, sensory-aware, and beginner-friendly environment.About the Teacher:Alexis Riley (she/they) is a white disabled/autistic psychiatric survivor and interdisciplinary performance artist from Shawnee and Osage Land (colonial West Virginia). Her participatory and community-created performance events blend disability culture, creative movement, and improvisation to celebrate the wisdom of divergent bodies. This work has been presented nationally and internationally at the Center for Mad Culture (Chicago, IL), the Cohen New Works Festival (Austin, TX) and the Edinburgh Festival Fringe (Edinburgh, UK), as well as at numerous universities. Critics have described these performances as "revolutionary," and "theatre of the future." A 2021 Charlotte W. Newcombe Fellow and recipient of a 2023 President's Postdoctoral Fellowship in theatre and drama, Alexis is currently an Assistant Professor of Theatre Studies at the University of Michigan. To learn more, visit www.madmoves.org (http://www.madmoves.org/)Accessibility: If you require an accommodation for effective communication or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact us with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7–10 days in advance of the event.

Please RSVP for the gallery tour here (https://forms.gle/sgqohhcYHKPAcRJ87).About the ComposerComposer Elliott Carter (December 11, 1908 - November 5, 2012) is internationally recognized as one of the most influential American voices in classical music, and a leading figure of modernism in the 20th and 21st centuries. He was hailed as "America's great musical poet" by Andrew Porter and noted as "one of America's most distinguished creative artists in any field" by his friend Aaron Copland. Carter's prolific career spanned over 75 years, with more than 150 pieces, ranging from chamber music to orchestral works to opera, often marked with a sense of wit and humor. He received numerous honors and accolades, including the Pulitzer Prize on two occasions: in 1960 for his String Quartet No. 2 and in 1973 for his String Quartet No. 3. Other awards include Germany's Ernst Von Siemens Music Prize and the Prince Pierre Foundation Music Award. Carter was the first composer to receive the United States National Medal of Arts, and is one of a handful of composers inducted into the American Classical Music Hall of Fame. He was recognized twice by the Government of France: being named Commander of the "Ordre des Arts et des Lettres," and receiving the insignia of Commander of the Legion of Honor in September 2012. About the PerformersLeighton Fong, a longtime member of San Francisco's Left Coast Chamber Ensemble, is Principal Cellist of the California Symphony, and has taught at UC Berkeley for over thirty years. He plays regularly with Eco Ensemble and Empyrean Ensemble, and was a member of the San Francisco Contemporary Players. In addition to specializing in contemporary music, he has performed the complete string quartets of Beethoven with the Los Angeles based Southwest Chamber Music Society and the complete string quartets of Schubert on original instruments with the Berkeley Schubert Quartet. Leighton studied at the San Francisco Conservatory, the New England Conservatory, the Bern Conservatory in Switzerland, and the Royal Danish Conservatory in Copenhagen, Denmark. Born in Sacramento, California, he has lived in Berkeley since 1991. Rohith Karur is a Ph.D. student in the Physics Department at UC Berkeley and at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. He completed his undergraduate education in physics at UC Berkeley. Rohith has been playing the violin for 21 years. Michael Arumainayagam is a 5th year Ph.D. student in the Physics Department at UC Berkeley. He studied Chemistry and Physics as an undergraduate at Harvard University. Michael has been playing the cello for 19 years. About the exhibitionNancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. events.description: Born in the wake of China's controversial one-child policy, six-year-old Wang Juan (Cao Ruofan) finds her life completely upended by her mother's pregnancy. The young girl is soon taken from her rural home���where kite flying and swimming fill her days—and brought to the home of a discordant, childless couple. Abandoned in an unfamiliar city with her new legal guardians, Juan strives to find a sense of belonging, a struggle that only worsens when she's uprooted twice more before turning eighteen. Anchored by a powerful performance from Resurrection's Li Gengxi, who plays teenage Juan, Zou Jing's confident debut is an achingly tender coming-of-age drama. And while it never shies away from the harrowing realities of the political directive that dehumanized and haunted so many, A Girl Unknown also reaffirms the undeniable, striking hopefulness of a young person's belief in love and self.

events.title: Film Screening: The Dreamed Adventure
events.description: The winner of the Jury Prize at this year's Cannes Film Festival, German director Valeska Grisebach's first feature since 2017's Western deftly shape-shifts between genres. Yana Radeva plays Veska, a Bulgarian archeologist who runs into an old love, Said (Syuleyman Letifov), who is involved in some legally murky business dealings. When he goes missing, Veska investigates, leading to a labyrinthine border town mystery full of intrigue and local color. The Dreamed Adventure finds Grisebach once again working with a nonprofessional cast to create a film with the grit of a Western and the scope of Chinatown. One could happily get lost in the movie's intoxicating atmosphere—or instead focus on Radeva's layered performance as a woman enmeshed in a slow-burn thriller that she might not come out of alive. But above all, the drama creates a portrait of a little-seen world brought to vibrant life by Grisebach and actors who know the region's riddles and dangers like the back of their weathered hands.

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: Freeness for the G-circulant Decomposition of the Partial Transposeof Random matrices
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Octavio Arizmendi, CIMAT GuanajatoWe study the asymptotic distribution of the Partial Transpose of Random Unitarily Invariant Random Matrix Ensembles from a new perspective. We introduce a left $G$-circulant decomposition for matrices indexed by an arbitrary finite group $G$, extending the diagonal decomposition associated with cyclic groups. We show that, when $A\in M_{|G|}(\mathcal A)$ is free from $M_{|G|}(\mathbb C)$, the components arising from the left $G$-circulant decomposition of $A^t$ form a free family with the components associated with inverse pairs forming $R$-diagonal pairs. We also describe the distributions of these components in terms of the distribution of $A$. Our results recover the cyclic case and show that different group structures of the same order may lead to different free decompositions of the same matrix. This is joint work with Julian Zazuela-Obeso.

events.title: Critical Conversations: Transforming the Field of Black Studies with Selina Makana
events.description: Materialist Nationalism: Challenging the Heroic Masculinist Rendering of the Nation Nation building exists in an uneasy and fraught relationship with women. On the one hand, nations revere women for their social reproductive labor. In twentieth-century Africa, nationalist movements deployed the figure of "Mama Africa" to galvanize the masses for the fight for independence. On the other hand, women and girl women's bodies were used as battlefields in wars and political repression in the colonial and postcolonial period, albeit in different ways. This lecture focuses on Selina Makana's new book, Beyond the Battlefield: Women and the Nation in Twentieth-Century Angola (https://www.ohioswallow.com/9780821426739/beyond-the-battlefield/), to examine the meanings and complexities of Angolan women's lived experience of war and militarism and reveal the extraordinary means by which they contend with and contest the politics of the nation. Selina Makana is an Assistant Professor of African history at the University of Memphis. Her research and teaching interests focus on African history, gender and militarism, and African diaspora studies. Her first monograph, Beyond the Battlefield: Women and the Nation in Twentieth-Century Angola (Ohio University Press, 2026), probes the relationship between women, war, and nationalist politics in Angola. She is currently working on her second book project Paranoia and Pathology in the Colony: Hygiene, Health, and Colonial Governance in Early Twentieth-Century Angola, that examines the entwined histories of public health and colonial governance in Angola. She has published articles in Meridians: Feminism, Race, Transnationalism; Gender and History; and The Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African Women's History.

events.title: TAC Seminar - Tara Dacunha (Stanford)
events.description: Title: Enabling precision inference on dark matter with robust subhalo population modelingAbstract: The small scale structure of dark matter is an emerging frontier for precision cosmological inference on dark matter physics. The near-field universe can provide powerful constraints through tracers of the underlying population of low mass dark matter "subhalos": faint dwarf galaxies, gravitationally-impacted cold stellar streams, perturbed strong lenses, and annihilation/decay flux sources. However, in order to turn these tracer populations into robust dark matter constraints, it is necessary to model the connection between the theoretically understood population of dark matter halos falling into the potential well of a galaxy and the uncertain tidally evolved subhalo population probed by these observables. Any constraint on deviation from the standard cold dark matter (CDM) paradigm implies a thorough and precise understanding of what CDM predicts at these small nonlinear scales, an understanding that currently lacks consensus and remains rife with unquantified modeling uncertainties. We present SubMERGE, a physically motivated analytical subhalo evolution model tested on cosmological simulations with and without disks, accounting for the numerical limits of the simulations and propagating learned uncertainties. This model builds on our new measurements of a universal profile shape for tidally evolving subhalos across simulations. Applying the model to cosmological simulations allows us to leverage their realism to generate various realizations of subhalo populations by modeling numerically unreliable subhalos. Crucially, without running new simulations, SubMERGE can flexibly explore the impact of altering tidal mass loss for different halo or disk growth histories as well as different density profiles for cases of dark matter self-interactions or baryonic effects. SUBMERGE has broad applicability to analyses that require fast, flexible, and realistic evolved dark matter subhalo populations. We present predictions for present day subhalo properties of Milky Way-mass hosts with implications for dark matter inference with dwarf galaxies, stellar streams, strong lenses, and annihilation/decay searches.Host: TBD

events.title: Condensed Matter Seminar with Alfred Q.R. Baron: Investigation of Mesoscale Liquid Dynamics via sub-meV Resolution Inelastic X-Ray Scattering
events.description: Investigation of Mesoscale Liquid Dynamics via sub-meV Resolution Inelastic X-Ray Scattering The dynamic structure factor, S(q, w), of liquids undergoes dramatic changes as q increases: the classic Rayleigh-Brillouin triplet is overcome by viscous relaxations, which then dominate the spectral lineshape, preserve the acoustic mode to higher q and give it both a higher sound velocity and narrower linewidth. However, it is difficult to measure this region as light scattering does not reach high enough q and neutron scattering does not reach low enough q. We have developed inelastic x-ray scattering with world-leading resolution to probe this mesoscale region. We will present results from water, explaining a decades-old controversy, and then isolating several components of the viscous relaxation using a modal decomposition of a generalized Langevin model. This is a step toward a consistent approach to mesoscale liquid dynamics, including the determination of the time and length scales of viscous relaxation processes.

events.title: Designing a quasi-experiment to study the clinical impact of adaptive risk prediction models (Gabriel Zayas-Cabán, University of Wisconsin-Madison)
events.description: Title: Designing a quasi-experiment to study the clinical impact of adaptive risk prediction modelsAbstract: Clinical risk prediction is a valuable tool for guiding healthcare interventions toward those most likely to benefit. Yet, evaluating the pairing of a risk prediction model with an intervention using randomized controlled trials presents substantial challenges, making quasi-experimental designs an attractive alternatives. Existing designs, however, assume that both the model and the decision rules used to trigger interventions (typically a risk threshold) remain fixed. This limits their utility in modern healthcare, where both are routinely updated. We introduce a regression discontinuity framework that accommodates adaptation in both the model and the risk threshold. We precisely characterize the form of interference introduced by these adaptations and exploit this structure to establish conditions for identification and thus design estimation strategies. The key idea is to define counterfactual risks-the scores patients would have received under hypothetical reorderings-thereby restoring local exchangeability and enabling valid estimation of the local average treatment effect. Our estimator leverages the fact that, although counterfactual risk vectors grow with time, they typically lie in a low-dimensional space. In simulations of cardiovascular prevention programs, we show that our method accurately recovers treatment effects even as thresholds adapt to meet operational or clinical targets and models are updated to align predicted and observed outcomes or to exclude demographic predictors such as race.Bio: Gabriel is an Associate Professor in the Industrial and Systems Engineering Department at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. He also holds an affiliate appointment with the BerbeeWalsh Department of Emergency Medicine in the School of Medicine and Public Health. His work spans healthcare delivery, stochastic modeling and optimization, and causal inference. His recent focus is on causal inference methods to evaluate the use of predictive models in healthcare. Before coming to Wisconsin, Gabriel was a President's Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of Michigan and completed his Ph.D. at Cornell University's Center for Applied Mathematics, advised by Professor Mark E. Lewis. He received his B.A. in Mathematics from the University of South Florida.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Jared Shaw, Professor, UC DavisStereoselective Synthesis with Rhodium Carbenes and NitrenesLow-valent reactive intermediates of carbon and nitrogen—namely, transition-metal complexes of carbenes and nitrenes—display diverse and powerful reactivity in the synthesis of complex organic molecules. Our group has focused on rhodium carbene complexes derived from substrates that lack electron-withdrawing groups. The diminished electrophilicity of these intermediates imparts exceptional functional group tolerance, enabling the construction of architecturally complex organic frameworks. The development of new methods and their application to the synthesis of a variety of heterocycles, including several natural products, will be presented. In parallel, analogous transformations involving rhodium nitrenes have been employed to generate complex heterocycles. The discovery of the first five-membered aromatic heterocycles featuring point chirality within the ring will be described, along with discussion of their distinctive structural characteristics.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.title: What Do You Get for "Some College?" Intersecting Inequalities in the Returns to Unfinished Credentials
events.organizer: Center for Studies in Higher Education
events.description: While nearly 40% of entrants into bachelor's degree (BA)-granting colleges in the United States do not earn BAs within six years—yielding 2 million people considered "dropouts" each year—limited research examines the labor market returns to unfinished BAs. To what extent, and for whom, might earning some BA college yield labor market advantages? How do relative advantages or disadvantages to unfinished BAs variously reproduce and disrupt existing sociodemographic inequalities? We answer these questions using restricted-access data drawn from ELS:2002, investigating the payoffs to some BA college in early career wages and how they vary by categories of race and gender. We find that the wage premium to some BA college over those with either a high school diploma or those with some AA-granting college varies substantially by race, gender, and their intersection, with Black women benefiting most and White men experiencing wage penalties. Explanatory analyses reveal more granular explanatory mechanisms, including time spent in the labor market and total credits earned. Incorporating measures of debt into our models do not change the primary findings. We conclude by discussing the implications for understanding the relationship between higher education trajectories and labor market inequality. RSVP (https://forms.gle/SCxRAATNhQNuZEgv7) required.

events.title: Maria Carolina Tomás | Beyond Racial Boundaries? An Examination of Interracial Unions in Contemporary Brazil (Lecture)
events.organizer: Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies
events.description: Event Description Brazil is known for relatively high rates of interracial unions compared to other countries. Historically, these relationships have sometimes been interpreted as evidence of harmonious relations between racial groups. In this talk, Maria Carolina Tomás challenges this interpretation by examining interracial unions as both intimate relationships and sites where racial boundaries and inequalities may persist. Drawing on several national surveys as well as qualitative interviews, Professor Tomás analyzes changes and continuities in interracial union rates in Brazil over time, examining the role of geography, and family background on the likelihood of being in an interracial relationship. Further, her presentation will explore how unpaid domestic labor, racial discrimination within intimate relationships, as well as in interactions with family, friends, and people in public spaces, raise fundamental questions about whether interracial unions should be understood as a case of transcending racial boundaries or maintaining them.Professor Tom��s will also be offering a workshop for UC Berkeley graduate students later in the week by application only. More info: 10/15 Tomás Workshop (https://events.berkeley.edu/clacs/event/332501-maria-carolina-tomas-turning-toward-the-literary)Co-sponsored by the Department of Demography.Speaker Maria Carolina Tomás is a professor in the Graduate Program in Social Sciences at Pontifícia Universidade Católica de Minas Gerais (PUC Minas, Pontifical Catholic University of Minas Gerais) and coordinator of the Specialization Course in Integrative and Complementary Health Practices at the Instituto de Educação Continuada (Institute for Continuing Education) at PUC Minas. She holds a B.A. in Social Sciences and M.A. in Demography from the Federal University of Minas Gerais (2004), as well as M.A. and Ph.D. degrees in Sociology and Demography from UC Berkeley. Her main areas of expertise are social stratification, family, race, and education, and she is the author or co-author of over 40 articles and chapters in Revista Planejamento e Políticas Públicas, Revista Latinoamericana De Población, Revista Brasileira de Estudos de População, Revista Multidisciplinar De Estudos Científicos Em Saúde, among many others. More recently, she has turned to literary studies to think through the complex ways that Black Brazilians navigate the country's changing racial landscape and what that might tell us about whiteness, race, space, and social mobility in Brazilian society. Professor Tomás serves as co-editor of the Brazilian Journal of Population Studies, is member of the Evaluation Committee of Applied Social Sciences of Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de Minas Gerais (Research Support Foundation of the State of Minas Gerais), and co-coordinator of CP14 Sociology of Ethnic-Racial Relations of the Brazilian Society of Sociology. She also coordinated the Center for Evaluation and Research in Higher Education (NAPES) between 2015 and 2023 and was president of the Self-Assessment Committee (CPA/PUC Minas) during the same period. Professor Tomás also served as Research Coordinator of the Institute of Social Sciences at PUC Minas between 2023 and 2025. She was a member of the Fiscal Council (2019-2021) and the Board of Directors (2021-2023) of the Brazilian Sociological Society.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Cash Transfers in Developing Countries: Local Multipliers, Aggregate Effects, and External Adjustment"
events.description: Abstract:This paper studies the local and aggregate effects of cash transfers in developing countries, and how both change as the cash transfer program scales up. We build a two-region New Keynesian small open economy model and calibrate it to rich pre-treatment microdata from an ongoing cash transfer experiment in Malawi. The model implies a local multiplier on temporary transfers of about one, which depends on price stickiness, the share of liquidity-constrained households, and home bias in consumption. Spillovers to the rest of the country are negative under Malawi's restricted international capital mobility and parallel exchange rate regimes, as cash transfers appreciate the real exchange rate and reduce exports. Consequently, the aggregate multiplier is less than the local multiplier. As the program scales up, the local multiplier converges toward the aggregate multiplier, so a scaled-up program may have smaller multipliers than micro-level estimates suggest. However, with unrestricted capital mobility, spillovers can be positive, especially under a fixed exchange rate. These results highlight the importance of the macroeconomic policy environment for aggregate multipliers and the effects of scaled-up transfer programs.

events.title: Ukraine: The Frontline and The Future
events.description: Can Ukraine continue undermining Russian control of Crimea and Russia's ability to export oil and gas? Can Russia achieve a military breakthrough? Will Russia's efforts to mobilize more troops jeopardize Ukraine's ability to hold the frontline? By many accounts, Ukraine achieved more military successes in 2026 than it had in years. But this winter promises to be the most difficult yet– Russia has been steadily degrading Ukrainian energy infrastructure, and extensive blackouts are all but certain. In this talk, two experts from Kyiv will discuss the military situation, as well as the political and economic factors that will determine how Ukraine and Russia will fare this winter. The outcome of the next six months will be critical to positioning for negotiations in 2027. –Yevhenii Malik is a former Marine Infantry sergeant in the Armed Forces of Ukraine and a veteran of the Ukraine War. He has extensive frontline experience, having fought in Mariupol and across the Joint Forces Operation zone, where he led combat missions, amphibious operations, and coordinated tactical planning under extreme conditions. From April 2022 to September 2024, he endured captivity in Russia. Malik holds degrees in law, public administration, and a reserve officer qualification. He is recognized for his expertise in military leadership, crisis management, and strategic and tactical planning. Since October 2025 he has been the Head of National Security and Defense Education at the Kyiv School of Economics.Alexandra Vacroux is vice president for strategic engagement at the Kyiv School of Economics (https://kse.ua/). She develops partnerships with top faculty, schools, and programs around the world to help Ukraine train the human capital that it will need to survive and thrive after the war. She has been instrumental in standing up a new bachelor's in engineering with Olin College and is currently focused on building national security studies. Alexandra lived in Moscow from 1992 to 2004 and worked as a consultant for the Russian Privatization Agency, partner and head of sales at the Brunswick Warburg investment bank and was an active member of the board of United Way Moscow. She holds a Ph.D. in government from Harvard University and wrote her dissertation on corruption in Russian pharmaceutical markets. She was the Executive Director at the Davis Center for Russian and Eurasian Studies at Harvard from 2010 to 2025.

events.title: Discussion of The Savage Mind: An American Legacy
events.location: Native Community Center, Anthony Hall, UC Berkeley
events.description: "Ta-Nehisi Coates has written that race is the child of racism, not the father." Treuer goes on to argue that violence is ancestor to them both. He posits that frontier violence, begun as a colonial imperative, became an institutional mission carried out by American institutions, and once manifestation of America's destiny was achieved, the wave of frontier violence (the theft of Native land and the theft of black and, later, immigrant freedom) broke in two directions. It moved overseas and was expressed in US imperial policy in Cuba, Hawaii, Korea, and Viet Nam. And it moved inwards, into the very cultural fabric and composition of the republic and is re-expressed in the host of problems that beset us today from school shootings to the public execution of American citizens at the hands of the state.New York Times bestselling author and editor David Treuer is Ojibwe from Leech Lake Reservation in northern Minnesota. He is the recipient of a Pushcart Prize, three Minnesota Book Awards, and fellowships from the NEH, Bush Foundation, and the Guggenheim Foundation, and was a Fellow at the American Academy Berlin. Treuer's forthcoming book, The Savage Mind: An American Legacy, will be released on October 6, 2026. His most recent book, The Heartbeat of Wounded Knee: Native America from 1890 to the Present, was a New York Times bestseller, a National Book Award Finalist, a Minnesota Book Prize winner, a California Book Prize winner, a Los Angeles Times Book Prize finalist, and was a finalist for the Carnegie Medal. His work has appeared in The New York Times, The Los Angeles Times, The Washington Post, and Harper’s. He is a contributing writer for Atlantic Monthly Magazine and is an editor-at-large for Pantheon Books. He divides his time between his home on the Leech Lake Reservation and Los Angeles, where he is a professor of English at the University of Southern California.
