events.title: Seminar 237 - Macroeconomics/Monetary Economics: "Beyond Exposure: Predicting AI Adoption Based on Comparative Advantage"
events.description: Abstract: We document and explain the gap between measures of AI exposure and measures of AI adoption in the workplace. This leads us to propose a new AI adoption index based on comparative advantage. Using the representative German DiWaBe employee survey linked to worker and establishment information, we compare worker-reported AI use to prominent exposure measures and find that the relationship is weak. Motivated by this gap, we develop a framework in which adoption depends not only on technical feasibility (i.e., AI's absolute advantage measured by exposure) but on profitability (i.e., AI's comparative (dis)advantage relative to a specific worker), balancing AI productivity against AI user costs and worker productivity against wages. We operationalize this framework at the task level by (i) estimating worker productivity relative to pay, (ii) mapping exposure indices into AI productivity, and (iii) inferring task-specific AI user costs from revealed-preference adoption. The resulting occupation-level index accounts for almost 60% of cross-occupation variation in observed AI adoption, compared to 14% for an exposure-only model. The two approaches diverge substantially for approximately 30% of workers, highlighting that comparative advantage—not exposure alone—is crucial for assessing AI's labor-market impact.

events.title: Yuan T. Lee Lecture in Physical Chemistry
events.description: Toshi Suzuki, Professor, Kyoto UniversityReaction Dynamics in Solution Probed by Ultrafast PhotoemissionChemical reaction dynamics in aqueous solution have traditionally been studied using optical methods such as absorption, emission, and scattering spectroscopy. In this talk, I will describe our efforts to follow chemical reactions in solution in real time by detecting photoelectrons emitted from the surface of an aqueous solution—that is, by exploiting the photoelectric effect. At first glance, such measurements might appear to provide information only on processes occurring at the liquid surface. In practice, however, they also yield important insights into chemical reactions taking place in the bulk liquid. Furthermore, by combining photoelectron spectroscopy with infrared spectroscopy in a complementary manner, it becomes possible to track both changes in electronic states and accompanying changes in molecular structure. I will illustrate this approach mainly through examples involving nucleobases.

events.title: Archaeological Knowledge Under Threat
events.description: This talk will take place in person at the ARF and on Zoom.Register for online attendance here. (https://bit.ly/ARFtalks-2627) Doors will open at 4:30 PM for light refreshments. The program will start at 5:00 PM.Abstract: Knowledge of how people interacted with each other and the environment in the past can inform our understanding of the future and help us address current challenges facing human populations, such as migrations, resource depletion, and climate change. Knowledge generation in archaeology relies on vast amounts of information collected through excavation, survey, laboratory analysis, community engagement, and archival research to name a few. Destruction of information sources, thus, has far-reaching impacts on our understanding of the past, present, and future. This panel explores contemporary threats to archaeological knowledge production and knowledge curation. Some threats, such as looting and climate change-driven disruptions, can have obvious destructive impacts. Looting of sites causes widespread physical damage and loss of context for the stolen objects. Climate change, whether erosion, sea level rise, fires, or displacement of populations, also causes physical damage to archaeological remains. Other threats to our understanding of the past can be much more abstract and less visible. These include regulatory changes, financial disruptions, professional incentive systems, and even the algorithmic processes behind generative AI. Even if sites are spared from physically destructive impacts, the information they contain may still be at threat even after careful excavation. Panelists will reflect on these dramatic shifts in the physical and intellectual landscape of archaeological knowledge production and discuss approaches to mitigating the loss of information in archaeological research. About the speakers:Morag M. Kersel is professor of anthropology at DePaul University in Chicago. She is an archaeologist who works in the Eastern Mediterranean in the Neolithic, Chalcolithic and Early Bronze Age periods. Morag is interested in the relationship between cultural heritage law, archaeological sites and objects, the antiquities trade, and local interaction with cultural heritage. Eric C. Kansa is Program Director for Open Context (https://opencontext.org), an open access data publishing service for archaeology. His research explores policy issues relating to intellectual property, including Linked Open Data, language model AIs, and cultural property concerns. James C. Wright held the William R. Kenan, Jr. chair and is professor emeritus in the Department of Classical and Near Eastern Archaeology, Bryn Mawr College, Pennsylvania. Currently he is Director of the University of Toronto Excavations at Kommos in Crete leading a master plan of conservation and planning renewed excavations to examine the stratigraphy, conduct chronometric, floral, faunal, micromorphological, and soil research in 2028-2030. In Images Documenting Looting in the North Cemetery at Abydos, Egypt. https://opencontext.org/media/03fc3daf-9e17-489c-ba1b-624fd2f04cf3 (https://opencontext.org/media/03fc3daf-9e17-489c-ba1b-624fd2f04cf3) CC-BY

events.title: Indranil Chakravarty | The Power of Intercultural Dialogue: Octavio Paz between Mexico and India
events.description: A talk by Indranil Chakravarty (https://indrachakra.com/), film historian, screenwriter, and author, based on his new book, The Tree Within: Octavio Paz's Years in India (https://0235947a.streak-link.com/C3VGHy6fX8I10Qk1JABJW9Rn/https%3A%2F%2Fwww.amazon.com%2FTree-Within-Mexican-Laureate-Octavio%2Fdp%2F0143471651%2F%3F_encoding%3DUTF8%26pd_rd_w%3DF95xZ%26content-id%3Damzn1.sym.4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631%253Aamzn1.symc.5a16118f-86f0-44cd-8e3e-6c5f82df43d0%26pf_rd_p%3D4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631%26pf_rd_r%3DVR6CA1607Z5S9X17FJWB%26pd_rd_wg%3Dvlupw%26pd_rd_r%3D12aba704-4be6-41aa-b6f0-8da866b68464%26ref_%3Dpd_hp_d_atf_ci_mcx_mr_ca_hp_atf_d), that explores how Octavio Paz's years as Mexico's ambassador to India transformed his personal life, poetry, philosophy, and understanding of cultural exchange. Event moderated by Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor of Global Modern Art and South and Southeast Asian Art, UC Berkeley.The Tree Within (https://www.amazon.com/Tree-Within-Mexican-Laureate-Octavio/dp/0143471651/?_encoding=UTF8&pd_rd_w=F95xZ&content-id=amzn1.sym.4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631%3Aamzn1.symc.5a16118f-86f0-44cd-8e3e-6c5f82df43d0&pf_rd_p=4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631&pf_rd_r=VR6CA1607Z5S9X17FJWB&pd_rd_wg=vlupw&pd_rd_r=12aba704-4be6-41aa-b6f0-8da866b68464&ref_=pd_hp_d_atf_ci_mcx_mr_ca_hp_atf_d) is the enchanting story of Octavio Paz's passionate love-affair with India where he served as Mexico's ambassador in the 1960s. Immersing himself in the country's rich cultural life and contemplative traditions, Paz travelled widely, forged deep friendships with some of India's finest minds, and produced several of his most inspired poetry and essays. It was here that he met the love of his life and experienced what he called his 'second birth'. In this richly textured and erudite work, Chakravarty reconstructs the inner journey of the poet by delving into multilingual archives, declassified diplomatic files, personal letters, and intimate interviews. Blending biography, cultural history, and literary criticism, The Tree Within is a luminous testament to the enduring alchemy between India and the world through one of the greatest writers of the 20th century.Indranil Chakravarty (https://indrachakra.com/) has taught film history and screenwriting over two decades at film institutes in India and abroad, and has made several documentaries. He studied at Presidency College (Calcutta), Escuela Internacional de Cine y TV (EICTV) in Havana, and earned PhD from Victoria University of Wellington, New Zealand. He has published extensively in international research journals about biopics, literary biography and cosmopolitanism. His earlier book publications include The New Latin American Cinema, India's Audiovisual Market, and one in Spanish titled Redescubriendo a Tagore. events.title: Shoshana Berger // Good Life Design is as Little Life Design as Possible
events.description: The Jacobs Institute for Design Innovation welcomes Shoshana Berger, writer, strategist, and cofounder of the Aged Intelligence Society. With a career spanning journalism, design, and storytelling, Shoshana has shaped how organizations communicate ideas that matter, from her leadership in marketing at IDEO to her role guiding content and communications at Notion. Her work sits at the intersection of design, culture, and meaning, exploring how we make sense of complex systems and, ultimately, our own lives. ​In her talk, Good Life Design is as Little Life Design as Possible, Shoshana will challenge the idea that every aspect of life needs to be optimized, engineered, or intentionally crafted. Drawing on her experiences across design, media, and writing, she will explore what it means to step back from constant self-improvement and instead create the conditions for a life that unfolds more naturally. Moving between themes of storytelling, technology, and mortality, she offers a perspective on how to navigate ambition, creativity, and constraint without overdesigning the human experience. ​Come ready to question the pressure to design everything, and consider what it might mean to leave more space for life to happen on its own terms. This event is free and open to the public. ……………….. ​Design Field Notes (https://jacobsinstitute.berkeley.edu/design-field-notes/?utm_source=luma) is a lecture series where we invite the public to the UC Berkeley campus for conversations with designers, makers and artists who are contributing to shaping the future through design.If you require accommodation for a disability for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Jacobs Institute staff atjacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu (mailto:jacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu)with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.description: Michael Pollan & Christof Koch: A Journey into Consciousness (https://calperformances.org/events/2026-27/speakers/michael-pollan-christof-koch-a-journey-into-consciousness/) Co-presented with the UC Berkeley Center for the Science of Psychedelics Best-selling author Michael Pollan has spent decades exploring what it means to be human, from the politics of food to the science of psychedelics. In his most recent book, A World Appears: A Journey into Consciousness, he examines the mystery of consciousness through scientific, philosophical, literary, spiritual, and psychedelic perspectives. Pollan will be joined for this event by renowned neuroscientist Christof Koch, and the two will discuss what consciousness is, why it remains so difficult to study, and how psychedelic research is reshaping the field. events.title: Kaiser/DeGruttola/Kim at CNMAT
events.description: Henry Kaiser is an American guitarist and experimental improvisor. Recording and performing prolifically in many styles of music, he has appeared on more than 650 albums since 1976, Kaiser is also an academy award nominated filmmaker and a scientific diver in the US ANTARCTIC PROGRAM. He has recorded and performed with a very wide range of artists. To name just a few: Derek Bailey, Evan Parker, Cecil Taylor, Wadada Leo Smith, Jerry Garcia, Marilyn Crispell, Jin-Hi Kim, Soo-Yeon Lyuh, Richard Thompson, Bill Frisell, David Lindley, Thomas Mapfumo, Victoria Williams, Barbara Higbie, Terry Riley, Sonny Sharrock, Herbie Hancock, Bob Weir, Jaojoby, D'Gary, and many many more. Cellist and improviser Danielle DeGruttola creates music by thinking across sound and image, organizing frequency space, timbre, color, resonance, and geometric form into richly layered improvisational environments. Her work moves freely through acoustic performance, live electronics, film, visual art, and virtual reality, transforming the cello into a responsive medium for building sonic worlds rather than simply playing within them. Her methodology treats sound as a physical, visual pigment; her longtime collaborators—including guitarist Henry Kaiser, media artist Claudia Hart, and her partner in sound manipulation, composer Edmund Campion—serve as the "canvas" or "counterweight" to her cello. Yoona Kim, born in Seoul, South Korea, is an ajaeng performer, vocalist, and composer based in Boston and active across Boston and New York. A polymath of musical styles, she builds a distinctive musical world that moves between tradition and experimentation, past and present. Rooted in the temporal sensibility and sonic foundation of Korean traditional music, her work draws from the deep emotional resonance of blues, the rhythmic pulse of old-time music, and the freedom of jazz, free improvisation, noise, and electronic music. Moving fluidly across musical traditions and practices, Kim is particularly difficult to define by any single genre or musical language. Through performance, composition, and collaboration, she explores new sonic possibilities across genres and forms. She has also collaborated with others to develop an electronic ajaeng, extending the instrument into new acoustic and electronic territories.

events.title: New Directions in Bangladesh Studies: Borders, Belonging, and the Lived Experience of Political Exclusion in South Asia
events.description: A panel discussion featuring recent scholarship on Bangladesh by Farhana Afrin Rahman (https://www.polis.cam.ac.uk/people/farhana-afrin-rahman) and Md. Azmeary Ferdoush (https://www.lboro.ac.uk/subjects/geography-environment/staff/azmeary-ferdoush/). The event will highlight and discuss their newly published books.Farhana Afrin Rahman: After the Exodus: Gender and Belonging in Bangladesh's Rohingya Refugee Camps (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/after-the-exodus/2DD28018FD5AAB92A1B5B7DD6A03F16E#fndtn-information) (Cambridge University Press, 2024): An examination of how forced migration from Myanmar to Bangladesh has reshaped Rohingya women's lives, identities, and gender relations in displacement. Drawing on 14 months of feminist ethnographic fieldwork in the Kutupalong-Balukhali refugee camp, the book explores how women navigate marriage, labor, humanitarian aid, and camp leadership while creating new forms of belonging, community, and agency. Md Azmeary Ferdoush: Sovereign Atonement: Citizenship, Territory, and the State at the Bangladesh-India Border (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/sovereign-atonement/3030482A4989ABA36336DAA230829917). (Cambridge University Press, 2024): An examination of the former border enclaves of Bangladesh and India—extra-territorial spaces created in 1947 and exchanged between the two countries in 2015. Drawing on ethnographic and historical research, Ferdoush explores how newly incorporated Bangladeshi citizens experienced this transition and why the state worked to smooth their inclusion into the sovereign project. The book offers a fresh perspective on territory, citizenship, governance, and sovereignty, introducing "sovereign atonement" as a way to rethink geopolitical and nationalist narratives in South Asia and beyond. Kirtana Dasa Mausert (https://www.linkedin.com/in/kirtana-dasa-mausert-296991a/) (PhD Candidate, Anthropology) and Patrick DeSutter (https://anthropology.berkeley.edu/patrick-desutter) (PhD Candidate, Anthropology) will serve as discussants. Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies and Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies, UC Berkeley. _________________DATE: Wed, Oct 14, 2026 TIME: 9 am Berkeley | Calculate your local time (https://www.thetimezoneconverter.com/)ZOOM: Register HERE (https://berkeley.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_dF16WXt4RBq7OOdeB1tQ4w) _________________ This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter)_________________AUTHOR BIOSFarhana Afrin Rahman (https://www.polis.cam.ac.uk/people/farhana-afrin-rahman) is an interdisciplinary scholar of international politics whose research examines gender, displacement, humanitarian governance, and women's political agency across the Global South. She is Assistant Professor in Politics and International Studies at the University of Warwick. She previously held a Leverhulme Early Career Fellowship at the University of Cambridge, where she also completed her PhD. Her first book, After the Exodus: Gender and Belonging in Bangladesh's Rohingya Refugee Camps (Cambridge University Press, 2024), won the 2025 L.H.M. Ling Outstanding First Book Prize from the British International Studies Association and the 2026 Global Division Outstanding Book Award from the Society for the Study of Social Problems, and was shortlisted for the 2026 BASAS Book Prize. Rahman has conducted extensive research and fieldwork across Asia, Africa, and the Middle East and has worked with organizations including UNDP, UN Women, and USAID. Read more about Dr. Rahman HERE (https://www.polis.cam.ac.uk/people/farhana-afrin-rahman). Md Azmeary Ferdoush (https://www.lboro.ac.uk/subjects/geography-environment/staff/azmeary-ferdoush/) is Lecturer in Geography and Environment at Loughborough University, UK, and Docent in Political Geography at the University of Oulu, Finland. A human geographer, his research focuses on borders, territory, sovereignty, citizenship, and migration, with particular attention to decolonial approaches to theory and method. He is the author of Sovereign Atonement: Citizenship, Territory and the State at the Bangladesh-India Border (Cambridge University Press) and currently leads the Leverhulme Trust-funded project Geographies of Example (2026–2030). He received the 2023 Stanley D. Brunn Junior Scholar Award from the American Association of Geographers and holds a PhD in Geography from the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa. events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Diana Martinez
events.description: During US colonial rule in the Philippines, reinforced concrete was used to the near exclusion of all other building materials. In Concrete Colonialism (Duke, 2025), Diana Martinez (Architecture) examines the motivations for and lasting effects of this forgotten colonial policy. Arguing that the pervasive use of reinforced concrete revolutionized techniques of imperial conquest, Martinez shows how concrete reshaped colonialism as a project that sought durable change through the reformation of environments, colonial society, and racialized biologies. Martinez locates the origins of this material revolution in the development of Chicago, highlighting how building this urban center atop exceptionally challenging geology made it possible to transform diverse global ecologies. She details how the material's stability, plasticity, strength, and other qualities served the shifting imperatives of the US colonial regime, playing a central role in defending territory, controlling disease, and constructing monuments to nation and empire. By describing a world irreversibly remade, Martinez urges readers to consider how colonialism persists — in concrete forms — despite claims of its conclusion. Martinez is joined by Matthew Shutzer (History). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: Eli Yablonovitch: Can Physics expedite artificial intelligence?
events.description: The dual quests – to understand intelligence as it arises in biology and to build it in machines of our own making – have been with us for nearly a century. While neuroscience and psychology seek to characterize intelligence in terms of underlying neural mechanisms and emergent behavior, we still lack a set of principles that can account for how the interactions of many neurons within a brain give rise to intelligent behavior. Meanwhile, modern AI is following a largely empirical path to create a new technology without scientific foundation. While the resulting algorithms exhibit intriguing behavior, the working principles are unknown, usage risks are incalculable, and the path to further development is unclear. The premise of this seminar is that the current century will see the emergence of a new scientific discipline – the Science of Intelligence – that seeks to elucidate universal principles that govern intelligent systems, be they biological or machine, and that this will provide both much needed insight in neuroscience and a solid foundation for technological development. The seminar will meet weekly, featuring speakers from across campus and elsewhere, who will share their views on the open questions, topics of study and debate, and relevant disciplines that a science of intelligence will encompass. Wednesday, October 14, 2026 Time: 12:00pm Location: 101 Weill hall Speaker: Eli Yablonovitch Affiliation: Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences, UC Berkeley (https://betr.berkeley.edu/director/eli-yablonovitch/)

events.title: PMB Seminar with Gautam Dantas | Understanding, Predicting, and Remediating Perturbations to Host-Microbe Interactions
events.description: Antibiotics can acutely and persistently compromise microbiome stability and resilience, enabling enhanced colonization of pathogenic microbes, and loss of host-beneficial functions from depleted commensals. We interrogate resistome, taxonomic, and functional dynamics of microbiota of humans, animals, soils, and built-environments via high-throughput functional metagenomic selections, whole metagenome and transcriptome sequencing, and isolate phenotyping and whole genome sequencing. We use these datasets to model and predict the impact of various biotic and abiotic perturbations on the transmission and evolutionary dynamics of diverse microbiomes and their resistomes across time and habitats, through application of generalized linear mixed models and machine learning algorithms. By integrating community-level analyses of microbiome perturbation and response, with mechanistic analyses of novel microbial resilience functions, we are improving the accuracy and sensitivity of genomics-based methods for diagnosing and treating pathogens and their resistance properties in the clinic and maintaining or rescuing healthy microbiome states.

events.title: IPSR Colloquium: Jasmin Brooks Stephens, "Reimagining Suicide Prevention for Black Youth: Advancing Strengths-Based Approaches"
events.location: Room 1102 Berkeley Way West, 2121 Berkeley Way, Berkeley, CA 94704, USA
events.description: Jasmin Brooks StephensAssistant Professor of Clinical ScienceDepartment of PsychologyUniversity of California, BerkeleyReimagining Suicide Prevention for Black Youth: Advancing Strengths-Based Approaches The crisis of suicide among Black youth and emerging adults has intensified in recent years, yet suicide prevention science has rarely examined how risk and protective processes may operate uniquely within this population. In this talk, I will present a program of research that reimagines suicide prevention by integrating the study of sociocultural risk with strengths-based pathways to psychological well-being. I will first review empirical findings demonstrating how racism-related stress, racial trauma, and other sociocultural pressures contribute to vulnerability to suicidal ideation and behavior among Black youth. I will then highlight protective processes that buffer suicide risk and promote positive mental health outcomes among Black youth. Building on this work, I will introduce the Black Youth Thriving Framework for Suicide Prevention, a strengths-based conceptual model that shifts the field beyond crisis-oriented intervention toward the proactive cultivation of developmental assets that support resilience and thriving. I will conclude by outlining a research agenda for advancing upstream, community-engaged prevention science that centers youth voice, integrates mixed-methods methodologies, and translates empirical findings into sustainable systems of care designed not only to prevent suicide, but to promote flourishing among Black youth. Dr. Jasmin Brooks Stephens is an Assistant Professor of Clinical Science in the Department of Psychology at the University of California, Berkeley. She earned her Ph.D. in Clinical Psychology from the University of Houston and completed both her predoctoral clinical internship and postdoctoral fellowship at Harvard Medical School/Massachusetts General Hospital. Grounded in strengths-based approaches, Dr. Brooks Stephens' research program examines the social and contextual risk and protective factors that shape the mental health trajectories of Black youth and emerging adults, with a focus on suicide vulnerability and racial trauma. The overarching goal of her research program is to develop and implement culturally responsive interventions, programs, and policies aimed at reducing racism-related stress, suicide, and health disparities in Black communities. Her work has been supported by several national organizations, including the Ford Foundation, American Psychological Foundation, American Psychological Association, and the P.E.O. Foundation. In recognition of her contributions to advancing mental health equity, Dr. Brooks Stephens was named to the 2025 Forbes 30 Under 30 list in Healthcare.

events.title: On the Margins? Neolithic Expansion in the Black Desert, Jordan
events.description: This talk will take place in person at the ARF and on Zoom.Register for online attendance here. (https://bit.ly/ARFtalks-2627) About: At first glance, the Black Desert of eastern Jordan might appear to be a landscape that only archaeologists, film crews, and Bedouin crews could love, but recent research demonstrates that prehistoric people occupied the region in far greater concentrations than previously thought. Aerial archaeology, including satellite imagery, piloted flyovers, and unpiloted aircraft (drones) dramatically changed our perspective on how many people lived and worked in the region. In this lecture we explore these new perspectives by critically examining the evidence for the built environment on the landscape, including the buildings, wheels, and the animal traps known as desert kites. Coupled with data from excavation, our analyses suggest that the Black Desert Neolithic was exploited intensively by people who hunted gazelle using the thousands of desert kites as well as tended flocks of domesticated sheep. Rather than a marginal zone with only temporary and ephemeral human visits, the past decade of field investigations demonstrates how prehistoric people moved through and occupied the region, with connections to Mesopotamia, the Levant, and Arabia.

events.title: Cheyenne Tretter: Private Arms, Public Consequences: Rethinking Arms Competition and War in the Age of U.S. Defense Industry Privatization
events.description: Events Add to Calendar iCal / Outlook The post-Cold War transformation of the U.S. defense industry has fundamentally altered the dynamics of global arms competition and the connection between arms racing and the risk of war. Cheyenne Tretter argues that increasing levels of privatization have transformed U.S. arms production by shifting arms racing from an episodic to a continuous phenomenon, and that this shift increases the risk of war by creating information problems that hinder adversaries’ ability to assess each other’s capabilities and intentions. To evaluate this argument, Tretter constructs a large-N dataset of U.S. weapons systems from 1900 to the present, with each system coded by domain, level of private involvement, and whether its development or modernization was initiated during a period of heightened tensions or relative peace. This dataset demonstrates a structural break: pre-1991 arms development clustered around crises and intense rivalries, whereas post-1991 development occurs continuously. Complementing this, qualitative case studies of Cold War missile racing, Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and U.S.–China competition in the Taiwan Strait test whether privatization increases the likelihood of war initiation, and further examine how privatization influences wartime adaptation.

events.title: EECS Colloquium with Partha Ranganathan: From Unicorns to Centaurs: Powering the AI Moonshot
events.description: Decades after President Kennedy stood at Rice University to articulate the moonshot of that generation, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as the defining "space age" of our decade, transforming all aspects of our lives. In this talk, we will discuss the "rocket engines" necessary to power this moonshot, including the deep co-design required across the entire computing stack. We will present vertically-integrated innovations in AI infrastructure that have already birthed a new cottage industry of "unicorns", ranging from physical data centers & hardware to software and cloud solutions, and identify the exciting opportunities ahead. We will then look forward to a future of "centaurs," symbiotic partnerships between human ingenuity and artificial intelligence, highlighting the opportunities and challenges when we use AI to optimize AI. We will conclude by discussing how responsible innovation for this AI moonshot will need to go beyond codesign across technical communities to also require collective cross-community engagement and collaboration. Partha Ranganathan is currently a VP and Technical Fellow at Google, where he is driving next-generation computing systems for the AI era. He has pioneered numerous impactful innovations touching billions of users, including widely adopted ideas across all mobile and cloud systems. He has published 100+ papers, is the co-author of the popular "Datacenter as a Computer" textbook, and is a co-inventor on 125+ patents. He has been recognized with numerous awards, notably: top 35 young innovators in the world by MIT Tech Review, top-15 enterprise technology rock star by Business Insider, IEEE & ACM Fellow, and Rice University outstanding young alumni & IIT Madras distinguished alumni awards. Fun fact: Partha is one of the few computer scientists to have an Emmy award!

events.title: MBN Seminar: Using fluorescent biosensors to understand how stimulated neurons meet their energy demands
events.description: Dr. Gary Yellen, Professor,Department of NeurobiologyHarvard Medical SchoolTitle: Using fluorescent biosensors to understand how stimulated neurons meet their energy demandsSummary: The biochemistry of energy metabolism has been known for over 50 years, but how metabolism is dynamically regulated in individual cells and cell types remains poorly understood. This challenge is especially important in the brain, where energy demand is exceptionally high and can change from second to second. This talk will show how we use quantitative fluorescent biosensor imaging to dissect the rapid metabolic responses of neurons to activity. In several types of neurons in the mouse brain, meeting the energy demands of activity does not depend on lactate shuttling from astrocytes, but instead on the direct utilization of glucose by neurons. The biosensor experiments are revealing the signals that rapidly activate neuronal glucose metabolism—mechanisms that may differ from the classical signaling pathways described for other cell types.

events.title: New Directions: Green Transitions
events.description: REGISTER The transition to a low-carbon economy is reshaping how societies produce and consume energy, with far-reaching implications for technology, industry, policy, and everyday life. Yet moving away from fossil fuels brings complex challenges around infrastructure, affordability, political economy, and the distribution of costs and benefits. This panel brings together advanced graduate students from UC Berkeley whose research examines the forces shaping green energy transitions around the world. Drawing on emerging scholarship spanning energy systems, technological change, environmental policy, and social equity, the discussion will explore how societies can navigate the opportunities and tradeoffs of decarbonization, and what is at stake for communities, economies, and the future of the planet. The panel will feature Nathaniel Dolton-Thornton, PhD candidate in the Energy and Resources Group; Janna Zou Huang, PhD Candidate in Sociology; and August Rud Jacobsen, PhD candidate in the Department of Environmental Science, Policy, and Management. Ken Alex, Director of Project Climate at the UC Berkeley's Center for Law, Energy and Environment (CLEE), will moderate. This event is co-sponsored by the UC Berkeley Department of Environmental Science, Policy, and Management (ESPM); the Energy and Resources Group (ERG); and the Center for Law, Energy and Environment (CLEE).PanelistsNathaniel Dolton-Thornton (https://www.dolton-thornton.com/) is a PhD candidate in the Energy and Resources Group at UC Berkeley. His research examines the political economy of critical minerals for energy transitions, with a focus on China and the United States. Before joining UC Berkeley, he served as an Assistant Researcher with Dean Kelly Sims Gallagher's Climate Policy Lab in The Fletcher School at Tufts University. He holds master's degrees from the universities of Oxford and Cambridge, and a BS from UC Berkeley.Janna Huang (https://sociology.berkeley.edu/graduate-student/janna-z-huang) is a PhD Candidate in Sociology at UC Berkeley. Her work spans economic sociology, organizational theory, science and technology studies, and climate politics. Broadly, her research investigates how organizations navigate uncertain regulatory contexts for corporate climate accountability. Specifically, her dissertation examines climate disclosure (regulatory standards for the collection and reporting of sustainability metrics on emissions and targets to investors and regulators) as a lens into how sustainability performance metrics emerged as a solution to regulatory deadlock over corporate climate governance. While climate disclosure is now mandated across major financial markets worldwide, companies overwhelmingly fixate on producing sustainability metrics, which remain decoupled from integrating these metrics into decarbonization. Janna's work is published in Social Forces, Wiley Interdisciplinary Reviews: Climate Change, Research in the Sociology of Organizations, and Technology in Society. Prior to graduate school, she earned a B.S. in Computer Science with honors in Science, Technology, and Society, and an M.A. in Sociology from Stanford University.August R. Jacobsen (https://sites.google.com/view/berkeley-enlab/team/august-rud-jacobsen/?pli=1&authuser=0) is a PhD candidate at the Department of Environmental Science, Policy, and Management and a member of the Energy and Environment Policy Lab. He studies the political economy of green industrial policy in Europe and the US, with his dissertation examining the interactions between policy design, corporate strategy, and technology choice. His work engages with multiple disciplines, including comparative political economy, sustainable transitions research, and heterodox economics. Prior to starting his PhD, he led the Policy Coordination Unit at the EFTA Secretariat in Brussels and supported the Norwegian Presidency of the UN Economic and Social Council. He holds an MPhil from the University of Cambridge and a Dual BA from Sciences Po and UC Berkeley.Ken Alex (https://its.berkeley.edu/people/ken-alex) is the director of Project Climate (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/research/clee/research/climate/projectclimate/) at the UC Berkeley's Center for Law, Energy and Environment (CLEE). From 2011 to 2018, Ken was a Senior Policy Advisor to Governor Jerry Brown, the Director of the Governor's Office of Planning and Research, and the Chair of the Strategic Growth Council. Before joining the Governor's Office, Ken was the Senior Assistant Attorney General heading the environment section of the California Attorney General's Office. From 2000 to 2006, Ken led the California Attorney General's energy task force, investigating price and supply issues related to California's energy crisis. Ken is a graduate of Harvard Law School and holds a B.A. in political theory from the University of California at Santa Cruz.

events.title: Neyman Statistics Seminar with Jingshen Wang: Agentifying AI Evaluation: What to Evaluate, When to Stop, and How to Estimate
events.description: Evaluating modern AI agents is increasingly costly and time-consuming, as benchmarking tasks can require long sequences of model calls and tool interactions. Can we reduce evaluation time and token cost without sacrificing model evaluation accuracy? We introduce an agentic evaluation framework that jointly and adaptively learns what to evaluate and when to stop, with a tailored estimator that preserves evaluation accuracy. The system jointly learns what tasks to evaluate and when to stop execution, while probabilistically randomizing and adapting these decisions to enable statistical correction. By "learning what tasks to evaluate," it uses historical evaluation traces to identify which benchmark tasks are most informative for estimating agent performance. By "deciding when to stop," it actively monitors each trajectory and probabilistically continues only when further execution is expected to provide sufficient additional information about the eventual outcome. We pair this agentic system with a tailored estimator that corrects for adaptive task selection and stopping. Our theoretical analysis shows that the resulting framework preserves model evaluation accuracy while improving precision for a given evaluation budget. Experiments on agent benchmarks show that our approach reduces both evaluation time and token cost while preserving accurate model evaluation results.

events.title: Seminar 291, Department Seminar joint with Labor: Stephen Redding (Stanford University) - A Network Approach to Geopolitics
events.description: Abstract: We develop a tractable framework for analyzing geopolitics as a network of coordination and strategic influence. Countries choose geopolitical actions that trade off domestic interests against incentives to align with connected countries. Prior to policy choice, they can make costly bilateral investments to influence one another, with effects that propagate directly and indirectly through the geopolitical network. We show that the equilibrium mapping from domestic interests to geopolitical actions admits a spectral representation, allowing international disagreements to be decomposed into latent geopolitical cleavages. We further establish that the covariance matrices of domestic interests and geopolitical actions identify the underlying geopolitical network through its eigencomponents. We implement the framework using data on countries' domestic interests and geopolitical actions. The inferred network is low-dimensional, aligns with external measures of geopolitical ties, and recovers well-known historical cleavages, from the Cold War division between the Western and Soviet blocs to the contemporary U.S.–China divide. Counterfactual exercises show that geopolitical actions are determined not only by domestic interests and national capabilities, but also by countries' positions in the geopolitical network and by the direct and indirect propagation of strategic influence. See full paper here (https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/fw5k6xvlq2x7y11k9n5qa/SIGN_Paper.pdf?rlkey=b9zca1nh0maf64n5y3bmhnypq&e=2&dl=0).

events.title: Tokhang as Justice: Explaining the Urban Poor's Support for Rodrigo Duterte's Drug War [SEALIVES Keynote Address]
events.description: Speaker:Marco Garrido (https://sociology.uchicago.edu/directory/marco-garrido) (Associate Professor of Sociology, University of Chicago) The poor in Manila were the main targets of Rodrigo Duterte's drug war (Tokhang), and yet they strongly supported it. Current explanations of this support either discount it as the result of fear or misinformation or attribute it to instrumental or populist logics. I will argue that explaining support for the drug war in the communities most affected by it requires a better understanding of the communities themselves. We need to reconstruct the social worlds the poor inhabit and in which support for Tokhang makes sense. To this end, I conducted 53 interviews across six neighborhoods in Tondo, Manila, finding qualified support for the drug war. I propose understanding this support in terms of the demand and supply of social order within these communities. Whereas the drug war tends to be portrayed as having been orchestrated from above—which, to be clear, it was—my findings suggest that it was also a bottom-up enterprise enabled by the support and participation of community members.Speaker Bio: Marco Z. Garrido is an associate professor in sociology at the University of Chicago. He is the author of The Patchwork City: Class, Space, and Politics in Metro Manila (https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/P/bo40850773.html). He is wrapping up a second book titled Bad Words: Corruption, Politics, and the Politics of Knowledge and beginning work on a third, an ethnography of democracy in the Philippines.

events.title: Time as Space
events.description: This lecture is part of the Howison Lectures in Philosophy series hosted by the Graduate Division. About this Lecture Augustine says, in Book 11 of his Confessions: "What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to him who asks, I know not." He never says anything like that about space. Nobody ever says anything like that about space. And (indeed) the thought that there is something infinitely deeper and more mysterious about the question of time than there is about the question of space is all over the place in the history of western philosophy. And all of this suggests that an understanding of time as space, or as somehow reducible to space, or as somehow emerging from space, might represent a significant advance in our understanding of the world. And I want to argue here that an offhand remark at the end of an old paper by D. C. Williams – a remark that gestures in the direction of a far more radical and less familiar version of what is often referred to as the "spatialization" of time in the modern physical project – contains the kernel of an understanding like that.About David Z. AlbertDavid Z Albert is the Fredrick E. Woodbridge Professor of Philosophy at Columbia University in New York City. He has written extensively on various issues at the foundations of physics – particularly on the foundations of quantum mechanics and the direction of time. He received his Ph.D. in theoretical physics from the Rockefeller University in 1981, and his books include Quantum Mechanics and Experience, Time and Chance, After Physics, and A Guess at the Riddle. He is currently at work on a book about relationalism.

events.title: Stefanie Schulte Strathaus: Modes of Archivism
events.description: October 14–18, 2026 We welcome Stefanie Schulte Strathaus from Berlin as our guest for one week. She will speak about different facets of the curatorial work she has been involved with through the years and share several recent restoration projects completed by film archives in Germany, Egypt, and Nigeria. Much of her career has been spent at Berlin's Arsenal Filminstitut, where she is the Artistic Director and has helped lead the institution through its relocation to the Silent Green Kulturquartier in Wedding, uniting its film collection, administrative offices, and new cinema in one location. Schulte Strathaus is recognized for the programs she has helped develop and nurture, including the Berlinale's Forum and Forum Expanded; Arsenal Filminstitut's Living Archive project; Archival Assembly, a biennial festival; and publications such as Accidental Archivism. She serves on the Executive Committee of the International Federation of Film Archives, as well as the boards of the Harun Farocki Institut, Network of Arab Alternative Screens, and the master's program in film culture at the University of Jos, Nigeria. We celebrate her visionary curatorial work and leadership role within the international community through this series of special presentations and talks, including the Mosse Lecture on October 16.

events.title: Aaron Gitler: Granulin loss and TMEM106B risk converge on lysosomal C-terminal fragment pathology in frontotemporal dementia
events.description: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is the second most common cause of dementia after Alzheimer disease. Mutations in GRN, which encodes progranulin, are a major cause of FTD. Common genetic variants in the TMEM106B gene modify risk of FTD and the effect is especially strong in GRN mutation carriers. Intriguingly, in GRN mutation carriers, being homozygous for the protective TMEM106B haplotype seems to confer near lifetime protection against FTD. Despite the strong genetic link between GRN and TMEM106B, how these two genes interact mechanistically has remained unresolved. Recent studies have revealed that a C-terminal fragment of TMEM106B forms amyloid fibrils and accumulates in the brains of older individuals and patients with neurodegenerative disorders, including FTD. How the production of this fragment connects to granulin deficiency is also unknown. Using lysosome immunoprecipitation, we show that granulin deficiency drives the accumulation of the TMEM106B C-terminal fragment within lysosomes in Grn-knockout mice and GRN-null human iPSC-derived neurons. Recombinant progranulin supplementation reduced TMEM106B C-terminal fragment accumulation. Isogenic neurons carrying the TMEM106B risk allele displayed allele-dose-dependent fragment accumulation that was reversible by progranulin. Structural and genetic analyses demonstrated that TMEM106B dimerization stabilizes the protein and limits C-terminal fragment formation. These findings define a lysosomal pathway linking granulin deficiency to TMEM106B C-terminal fragment accumulation and explain how protective TMEM106B alleles can confer resistance to FTD, even for GRN mutation carriers.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: Leading When Energy Is Low: Self-Leadership Tools for Change, Stress, and Uncertainty (2026 Fall NOW Encore Series)
events.description: 2026 NOW Encore Series (https://hr.berkeley.edu/development/career-development/workshops) Periods of change, constraint, and constant adaptation place invisible demands on all of us—especially those in leadership and informal leadership roles. When energy is depleted, even highly capable professionals can find themselves reacting rather than leading, withdrawing rather than collaborating, or questioning their effectiveness. This session introduces an energy-based self-leadership framework that helps participants understand how they show up under pressure—and how that impacts decision-making, communication, and change readiness. Rather than focusing on fixing people or increasing output, we'll explore how energy and mindset shape leadership behavior in real time. Participants will examine common stress-response patterns that emerge during high workload, uncertainty, or organizational change, and learn how to interrupt unhelpful cycles before they cascade into burnout, disengagement, or conflict. Through reflection, live polling, and applied examples from higher education and healthcare environments, attendees will gain practical tools to lead themselves more consciously—even when circumstances are not ideal. This session is especially relevant for supervisors, managers, and staff who influence others without formal authority. The emphasis is on self-leadership as a prerequisite for sustainable leadership: cultivating awareness, flexibility, and agency so individuals can respond to change with clarity rather than depletion. Participants will leave with actionable strategies to stabilize energy, improve communication under stress, and lead with intention during times of ongoing change.Learning Outcomes: –Recognize how stress and burnout influence leadership behaviors and communication. –Identify their default energy patterns during pressure and change. –Apply at least one self-leadership strategy to respond more intentionally in challenging situations.Registrants will be sent a Zoom link and bCal invite as the virtual workshop date draws near.

events.title: Bancroft Library Roundtable
events.description: The UC Berkeley Library's Preservation Department recently completed the conservation of more than 35 prints for an exhibition at The Bancroft Library. The preservation team and Bancroft curators sought to balance the conservation needs of the prints with their history as active broadsides. In this talk, the conservators will discuss their conversations with curators about various approaches to respecting the integrity of the object; why certain types of damage, but not others, are addressed; and how these decisions reflect an effort to respect the goals of the printer as well as the presence of the human hand in the creation and collecting of the art object.

events.title: Graduate Workshop with Maria Carolina Tomás | Turning Toward the Literary
events.organizer: Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies
events.description: Event Description In this informal discussion of work-in-progress, Professor Maria Carolina Tomás invites graduate students working in literary studies, as well as students interested in thinking with literature, to ask broader questions about Blackness and lived experience in the African Diaspora. Specifically, she will share her new work on Jeferson Tenório, focusing on narrative strategies, narrators, and plotting, to think through the complex ways that Black Brazilians navigate changing racial dynamics in the country. Tenório is one of the most influential voices in Brazilian literature, a position consolidated by his winning the Jabuti Prize in 2021 for his novel O Avesso da Pele, and race constitutes a central theme in his work. His Black characters confront processes of racialization that permeate schools, workplaces, family relationships, romantic relationships, and interactions with public institutions. Racism is presented both in its explicit manifestations and through everyday practices, forms of constraint, silencing, suspicion, and mechanisms of control over Black bodies. In this project, Facing the White World: Blackness in De Onde Eles Vêm, Professor Maria Carolina Tom��s analyzes Tenório's novel, De Onde Eles Vêm, which has as its backdrop the entry of the first beneficiaries of affirmative action into the Brazilian university system. The discussion will focus on the author's choice of a first-person narrator as a way of presenting Black subjectivity and masculinity as lived and embodied experiences, as well as on his use of different contrasts throughout the novel to problematize the protagonist Joaquim's trajectory of social mobility, in a context that involves a transition from a predominantly Black world of origin to a predominantly white one in the university. This narrative strategy demonstrates how the protagonist experiences direct confrontations as well as moments of silencing, marking boundaries and hierarchies in his encounters with whiteness throughout his trajectory of social mobility, made possible by access to higher education through affirmative action policies. Professor Tomás will also share her experiences of being trained in the doctoral programs in Sociology and Demography at UC Berkeley and her recent studies in the Literature Department at PUC Minas and invites participants to share their own work and experiences with interdisciplinarity.Dr. Tomás will also give a public lecture on Monday 10/13. More info here: 10/13: Tomás Lecture (https://events.berkeley.edu/clacs/event/332487-maria-carolina-tomas-beyond-racial-boundaries-an).Co-sponsored by the Department of Spanish & Portuguese. Speaker Maria Carolina Tomás is a professor in the Graduate Program in Social Sciences at Pontifícia Universidade Católica de Minas Gerais (PUC Minas, Pontifical Catholic University of Minas Gerais) and coordinator of the Specialization Course in Integrative and Complementary Health Practices at the Instituto de Educação Continuada (Institute for Continuing Education) at PUC Minas. She holds a B.A. in Social Sciences and M.A. in Demography from the Federal University of Minas Gerais (2004), as well as M.A. and Ph.D. degrees in Sociology and Demography from UC Berkeley. Her main areas of expertise are social stratification, family, race, and education, and she is the author or co-author of over 40 articles and chapters in Revista Planejamento e Políticas Públicas, Revista Latinoamericana De Población, Revista Brasileira de Estudos de População, Revista Multidisciplinar De Estudos Científicos Em Saúde, among many others. More recently, she has turned to literary studies to think through the complex ways that Black Brazilians navigate the country's changing racial landscape and what that might tell us about whiteness, race, space, and social mobility in Brazilian society. Professor Tomás serves as co-editor of the Brazilian Journal of Population Studies, is member of the Evaluation Committee of Applied Social Sciences of Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de Minas Gerais (Research Support Foundation of the State of Minas Gerais), and co-coordinator of CP14 Sociology of Ethnic-Racial Relations of the Brazilian Society of Sociology. She also coordinated the Center for Evaluation and Research in Higher Education (NAPES) between 2015 and 2023 and was president of the Self-Assessment Committee (CPA/PUC Minas) during the same period. Professor Tomás also served as Research Coordinator of the Institute of Social Sciences at PUC Minas between 2023 and 2025. She was a member of the Fiscal Council (2019-2021) and the Board of Directors (2021-2023) of the Brazilian Sociological Society.

events.title: REI Colloquium: Mobilizing Action: The Role of Hope and Fear in Immigration Activism
events.description: Mobilizing Action: The Role of Hope and Fear in Immigration Activism My book project, Peril and Promise: Catalyzing Political Action Among Latinxs, is centered on citizen activism and revisiting the role of threat as a catalyst for political participation. Focusing specifically on the case of Latinx communities in the U.S., anti-immigrant threats have often been depicted as a necessary and sufficient ingredient for piques in political participation for Latinx communities—communities with strong ties to immigrant community members. I focus on how this threat hypothesis overlooks the more nuanced political psychology that spurs political behavior. In other words, rather than analyzing the isolated effect of very visible threat policies that heighten one's sense of fear, it is important to capture the competitive nature of policy cues where oftentimes participants are simultaneously exposed to both threat and opportunity appeals—policy scenarios that trigger sentiments of fear and hope. Fundamentally, this project asks the following question: Under what conditions do combined policy threat and policy opportunity messages create more incentives for political activism than either scenario alone? Most of our theories on emotions in political science have largely focused on white electorates. My book contributes to the growing field of how communities of color process threats and opportunities in their environments. By borrowing from a broader understanding of risk appraisal research, the implications of a coupled-threat-and-opportunity strategy can avoid the downward spiral of negativity often plaguing the most disillusioned and underrepresented portions of an electorate. Instead of potentially exacerbating feelings of helplessness while only emphasizing a sense of urgency with a looming political threat, I test whether combining both threat and opportunity-based political alternatives may be the most effective strategy to motivate Latinx communities to take action.About the Speaker:Vanessa Cruz Nichols, PHD is an Assistant Professor of Political Science in the Department of Political Science at Indiana University. She is a faculty affiliate with the Latino Studies Program and Center for Research on Race and Ethnicity in Society at Indiana University. Her research interests are situated within American Politics, political participation, public opinion, public health and race and ethnicity politics. events.title: The neural basis of cuttlefish camouflage and social behavior
events.description: All animals form internal neural representations of the external world that guide their behavior. Cuttlefish, coleoid cephalopods related to octopus and squid, perform visually driven adaptive camouflage by dynamically altering the color, pattern, and texture of their skin to create an approximation of their surroundings – a process directly controlled by the brain. Thus, cuttlefish perform a remarkable sensorimotor transformation: they recreate what they see on their skin, generating a motor output that approximates the sensory input itself. In addition to camouflage, cuttlefish use their dynamic skin to communicate with conspecifics using a series of innate skin patterns that reveal the animal's internal state. We are using the cuttlefish skin behaviors to understand how the physical properties of the visual world are represented by patterns of neural activity in the brain, and how this representation is transformed into an approximation of the physical world on the skin. We have performed a series of experiments to develop the dwarf cuttlefish, Ascarosepion bandense, as a model to investigate the neural basis of camouflage and social communication. We have sequenced the genome, developed gene editing techniques, completed a 3D brain atlas, developed camouflage and social behavior paradigms, examined dwarf cuttlefish behavior in the wild, and adapted miniscopes for underwater imaging. Furthermore, we recently succeeded in generating transgenic cuttlefish that express genetically-encoded calcium indicators in the brain, permitting the live imaging of neural activity. We are now using these technologies to simultaneously record neural activity and measure behavior to uncover how visual information is deconstructed in the brain, and then reconstructed into an image of the physical world on the skin.

events.title: José del R. Millán: Brain-Computer Interfaces: Fostering Learning, Plasticity, and Recovery
events.description: BCI control is a skill, and every component of a BCI system must support the activity-dependent plasticity that underlies skill learning and consolidation—yet the non-stationarity of EEG signals makes it hard to give users the coherent, stable feedback this process requires. I will illustrate how BCI use itself fosters learning, plasticity, and recovery, from a brain-controlled wheelchair restoring mobility, to BCI feedback that accelerates perceptual learning of small visuomotor errors, to a motor rehabilitation protocol that produces significant and lasting recovery in chronic stroke patients. I will then present two complementary strategies for stabilizing the neural features that drive the BCI: an unsupervised, Riemannian-geometry-based algorithm that corrects for feature drift in real time and lets an expert user's control features give naïve users a head start; and a neuromodulation approach in which transcutaneous electrical spinal stimulation induces cortical inhibition that sharpens sensorimotor activation and speeds BCI skill acquisition. Together, these two orthogonal approaches—one algorithmic, one physiological—show how stabilizing the neural features underlying BCI control can strengthen learning, favor cortical reorganization, and improve outcomes for both able-bodied and clinical populations.

events.title: Magdalena Ugarte: Rethinking the Normative — Settler State Planning, Indigenous Law, and Grounded Legal Pluralism | City & Regional Planning Lecture
events.description: Planning theory widely acknowledges that planning is inherently normative. Yet Western values, ethical frameworks, and visions for the future continue to shape everyday planning practice. The deep connection between planning and Western law is crucial: it often labels planning practices that challenge Western definitions of property, public interest, land use, and decision-making authority as illegal. Territorial conflicts between settler nation-states and Indigenous peoples illustrate these tensions. Drawing on years of community-engaged research with Indigenous communities in Chile, Magdalena Ugarte explores these disputes as clashing legal orders. By centering Indigenous law and land relations, we can reimagine planning in settler colonial contexts — shifting from the domination of Western law to practices rooted in legal pluralism. About Magdalena Ugarte is an associate professor in the School of Urban and Regional Planning at Toronto Metropolitan University, where she teaches planning theory, public policy, social and community planning, and studio. Her work examines the relationship between planning, settler colonialism, and other forms of racialized dispossession, as well as how communities persistently excluded from planning plan for themselves. She is currently involved in collaborative, community-based research projects that focus on Indigenous planning in Chile and Black-centered, Black-informed planning practices in Canada. She is also leading curricular changes that seek to advance racial justice and Indigenous rights in planning education. This lecture is part of the Department of City & Regional Planning's fall lecture series.

events.title: Translation in the Qing Poetic Imaginary | Lecture by Nathan Vedal
events.description: This talk, introducing a forthcoming monograph (Translation, Emulation, and Manchu Literary Culture), will consider the institution of a Manchu translation program in the elite Hanlin Academy. A subset of literati at the Hanlin Academy, a training ground for officials and court scholars who passed the civil service exam at the highest level, underwent a three-year program of Manchu study culminating in a final translation exam. Knowledge of Manchu gained at the Hanlin Academy, while primarily intended for bureaucratic purposes and court scholarship, is also evident in the deployment of multilingual literary effects in Chinese poetic compositions. Within Qing literary-intellectual culture, the juxtaposition of Chinese and Manchu yielded a productive venue for literary creation and self-fashioning. Speaker Bio:Nathan Vedal is an associate professor in the Department of East Asian Studies at the University of Toronto, specializing in Chinese intellectual and cultural history. He received his undergraduate degree from the Curtis Institute of Music and his PhD in Chinese history from Harvard University. His first book, The Culture of Language in Ming China: Sound, Script, and the Redefinition of Boundaries of Knowledge (Columbia University Press, 2022), won the Morris D. Forkosch Prize from the Journal of the History of Ideas.

events.title: Munis D. Faruqui | Aurangzeb 'Alamgir and the Mughal Empire: A History Retold
events.description: Please join us for a special book launch celebrating Aurangzeb 'Alamgir and the Mughal Empire: A History Retold (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/aurangzeb-alamgir-and-the-mughal-empire/A6421F92BBEEBA78238E75F4D636E7C0), the new work by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director of the Institute for South Asia Studies and Professor of South and Southeast Asian Studies at UC Berkeley. In this compelling reassessment, Professor Faruqui offers a fresh and nuanced account of Aurangzeb's reign, illuminating the ambitions, conflicts, and political pressures that shaped the Mughal Empire at a pivotal moment in its history. The conversation will be moderated by Abhishek Kaicker (https://history.berkeley.edu/abhishek-kaicker), Associate Professor of History at UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, Oct 15, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall ————– ABOUT THE BOOKAurangzeb 'Alamgir (r. 1658–1707) was the last of the so-called 'great' Mughal emperors. He remains a controversial historical figure: castigated for religious intolerance and placed at the centre of a narrative of Mughal decline by some; considered a great Muslim hero by others. In this richly researched exploration of Aurangzeb 'Alamgir's life and times, Munis D. Faruqui contests such simplistic understandings to unearth a more nuanced picture of the emperor and his reign. Drawing on a large and varied archive, Faruqui provides new insights into the emperor's rise to power, his administrative and religious policies, and the role of the imperial eunuchate and harem. By unpicking the complex dynamics of a long reign, from Aurangzeb 'Alamgir's accession to the last weeks of his life and his eighteenth-century memorialisation, this remarkable new history cuts through the many myths that have obscured the extraordinary life story of Emperor Aurangzeb 'Alamgir. SPEAKER BIOMunis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/) is a historian and the holder of the Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies. His focus is on the Muslim experience in South Asia, especially during the Mughal period. His books include Princes of the Mughal Empire, 1504-1719 (Cambridge University Press, 2012), Expanding Frontiers in South Asian and World History, co-edited with Richard Eaton, David Gilmartin and Sunil Kumar (Cambridge University Press, 2013), and Religious Interactions in Mughal India, co-edited with Vasudha Dalmia (Oxford University Press, 2014). His most recent book is titled Aurangzeb 'Alamgir and the Mughal Empire: A History Retold (Cambridge University Press and Juggernaut Press, 2026). He is co-editor-in-chief, along with Ali Anooshahr, of the Journal of Mughal Studies. In 2014, Dr. Faruqui was one of three faculty recipients of UC-Berkeley's Distinguished Teaching Award. The award recognizes teaching that "incites intellectual curiosity in students, engages them thoroughly in the enterprise of learning, and has a lifelong impact." Dr. Faruqui is the current Director of both the Institute for South Asia Studies and the Global, International & Area Studies unit. In addition to the Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies, Dr. Faruqui is affiliated with the Department of History and the Department of Middle Eastern Languages and Cultures. events.title: BTLJ-BCLT Fall Race & Law Symposium – “Being Human in the Age of AI”
events.description: Join us for Being Human in the Age of AI, a symposium exploring how artificial intelligence is reshaping the law’s most basic assumptions about the human person — from the privacy of the mind to the boundaries of legal responsibility. Across four panels, we trace an arc from the innermost self outward: how neurotechnology and algorithmic design test the limits of cognitive liberty; how deepfakes and biometric systems unsettle the law of identity; how automated decision-making challenges due process and the right to be heard; and how courts and legislatures are struggling to define what AI fundamentally is. Attendees will hear from leading scholars, technologists, and practitioners grappling with these questions in real time, as courts issue rulings, states pass conflicting statutes, and AI companies themselves debate the moral status of the systems they build.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Risk Appetite and Monetary Transmission"
events.description: Abstract: We construct a new high-frequency measure of changes in risk appetite around Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meetings. Fed policy actions and communication have substantial effects on risk appetite, consistent with the literature on the risk-taking channel of monetary policy. Most of the variation in asset prices and risk appetite is unexplained by conventional interest-rate surprises, which points to an important role of risk appetite in monetary transmission. Proxy SVARs with two separately-instrumented monetary policy shocks—a risk-free rate shock and a risk appetite shock—show the empirical importance of this channel. Risk appetite shocks have large, significant, and theory-consistent effects on inflation, output and employment. By contrast, the effects of risk-free rate shocks become insignificant or switch signs as soon as a risk-appetite shock is included in the VAR setup. Our evidence suggests that monetary transmission works primarily through risk asset prices and risk appetite. Standard estimation of monetary transmission based solely on interest-rate surprises misses most of these effects for two main reasons: First, the impact of interest-rate policy on asset prices is time-varying and state-dependent. Second, central bank communication can affect risk appetite and asset prices in ways that go beyond changes in the expected policy path.

events.title: Jürgen Dinkel | All remains in the Family: A History of Inheritance in the US and Europe Since 1800
events.description: Over the next 25 years, Americans will inherit more than $100 trillion. Economists anticipate a "great wealth transfer" from the Baby Boomer generation to their children and grandchildren. At the same time, this enormous wealth will be distributed extremely unevenly throughout society. While a select few will inherit vast fortunes, many will inherit little, nothing at all, or even debt. This raises questions with renewed urgency—questions that have been debated in the transatlantic world since the American and French Revolutions: Who should receive a deceased person's estate? Who counts as family? Who should decide how an estate is distributed? How can the unequal distribution of inherited wealth be justified, and how can the rights to private property and equal opportunities be reconciled? In his lecture, Jürgen Dinkel traces the history of inheritance in the US and Europe since 1800. He demonstrates how governments, families, and individuals repeatedly negotiated the transfer and distribution of estates, thereby also renegotiating kinship relations, the bonds between the individual, the family, and the state, as well as the legitimization of wealth inequalities within their societies. Ultimately, this lecture contributes to the new histories of capitalism, the family, and the state, arguing that Euro-American societies from the 19th to the 21st century are fundamentally structured around inheritance and the family. Jürgen Dinkel is Professor of Modern and Global History at the University of Leipzig. His research focuses on the history of colonialism and decolonization, the Global South in World Politics, and European social history. His most recent publications include: Acknowledgments: The History of Academic Gratitude, in Bulletin of the German Historical Institute, Washington D.C. 76 (Fall 2025); "'The Rich Uncle from America': Transnational Inheritance Transfers between the United States, Germany, and Russia, 1840s–1980s," Law and History Review (2025); and "The Non-Aligned Movement: The Role of Diplomacy in Third-worldism and the Global South," in Oxford Handbook on the History of the Global South (Oxford UP, 2025). events.title: PMB Seminar with Adam Steinbrenner | Seeing like a plant: immune recognition and signaling by cell surface receptors
events.description: Plants sense extracellular cues through several hundred cell surface receptors. The most rapidly evolving group of receptors is the leucine-rich repeat receptor-like proteins (RLPs), which transduce immune signals as a bipartite receptor complex with the adapter SOBIR1. In recent years many new examples of immunogenic patterns detected by specific RLPs have been described, highlighting their versatility as immune sensing modules. I will discuss unique features of the RLP family that mediate recognition and signaling functions. For recognition, RLPs encode an extracellular island domain, which allosterically couples ligand binding to co-receptor recruitment. For signaling, RLPs lack a kinase domain typical of most receptors, but the short cytoplasmic tail domain can encode signaling through different defense pathways. For both recognition and signaling functions, I will describe new insights from our study of Inceptin Receptor (INR), which detects caterpillar-derived peptide elicitors and evolved 28 mya in a single subtribe of legumes. Since both island and tail domains are small (~10-60 aa) shared features of all RLPs, they may represent modular, editable handles to engineer plant immune systems.

events.title: Moving Ideas into Action in a Shifting Policy Landscape: A Symposium Marking Twenty Years of the Center for Law, Energy, and the Environment
events.organizer: Center for Law, Energy & the Environment
events.description: Join Berkeley Law’s Center for Law, Energy, and the Environment (CLEE) for a symposium marking the research center’s 20th anniversary. Berkeley Law established the Center for Law, Energy, and the Environment (CLEE) in 2006 – a time when California was launching bold, world-leading policies to address climate and environmental issues. At the same time, the federal government was walking back from its commitments and trying to limit the State’s authority. Fast forward twenty years and the policy landscape looks similar, albeit much more dire – both in the urgency of the climate crisis and the scale of federal rollbacks and attacks on state action. Over the past twenty years, CLEE has honed its focus and expertise in this shifting and dynamic policy landscape. A large portion of CLEE’s work has focused at the subnational level and has resulted in significant contributions from the local to global scale. This half-day symposium, marking the 20th anniversary of CLEE, welcomes new and long-time friends and partners of CLEE to discuss the challenges, impacts, and significance of environmental law and policy scholarship and how to make a difference in a dynamic policy landscape. Speakers include: Senator Henry Stern ‘09 (CA District 27) Professor Dan Farber, Founding Faculty Director of CLEE Rick Frank, Founding Executive Director of CLEE Rachel Morello-Frosch, Inaugural Associate Provost of Energy, Climate, and the Environment, UC Berkeley The symposium will be held from 2:00–5:00 p.m., and followed by a reception with drinks and hors d’oeuvres. We are grateful to our event sponsors, Brownstein, Nossaman, Orrick, Sheppard, The Tomblin Family Foundation, Willis Towers Watson, and Wilson Sonsini. We encourage you to RSVP at your earliest convenience due to limited space. events.title: Geography Colloquia Series - Salt Lakes: An Unnatural History
events.description: Salt lakes are some of the world's most extraordinary ecosystems, but nearly all of them―from the Great Salt Lake to the Aral Sea��are drying up, a harbinger of dust storms, rising sea levels, and worsening human health. Caroline Tracey's book Salt Lakes: An Unnatural History, a hybrid work of memoir and geographic research, spans the American West, Mexico, Argentina, Kazakhstan and beyond, documenting salt lakes, their loss, and the efforts underway to save them, as well as Tracey's relationships to the lakes. In this talk she will describe the making of the book, including how it draws on her training in geographic methods and on additional creative sources such as Mormon diaries, Soviet realist novels, Australian Aboriginal paintings, and techniques of memoir and the personal essay. Caroline Tracey is the author of Salt Lakes: An Unnatural History (W.W. Norton, 2026). After receiving her PhD in Geography from the University of California, Berkeley, she became an independent writer and journalist specializing in the Southwestern US, Mexico, and their borderlands. Her work has appeared in numerous publications and has received a Fulbright fellowship, the Waterston Prize for Desert Writing, an Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writer's Grant, and a Creative Capital State of the Arts Award.

Simon is the author of three books and many articles on the criminal legal system in the United States and its relationship to shifts in American society and democracy. events.title: (Screening) Omar Khan | Mohenjo Daro: Unsealing an Ancient Indus City.
events.description: Join us for a screening of Mohenjo-daro: Unsealing an Ancient Indus Cit (https://www.harappa.com/video/mohenjo-daro-unsealing-ancient-indus-city)y, a documentary that explores one of the world's greatest lost civilizations — the Indus Valley Civilization – through the eyes of Omar Khan, the founder of Harappa.com. Omar Khan walks through the nearly five thousand year old city of Mohenjo-daro, discusses recent speculations about the Great Bath and the so-called Stupa mound, and raises many unanswered questions about this Bronze Age civilization while sharing recent perspectives and information. High quality graphics, countless actual Indus seals, pottery and sculptures photographed by leading archaeologists like Drs. Jonathan Mark Kenoyer and Richard H. Meadow; new photography and rare archival images from the earliest excavators; a handful of key recreations of the Great Bath and Stupa-Mound; the voices and music of Sindh from premiere music studio Lahooti Live Sessions. Featuring interviews with leading scholars, this film is ideal for students, educators, and anyone curious about the ancient world and the Indus civilization, the original urban civilization which some 2 billion people can claim descent from in modern India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. The documentary is divided into five chapters: 1. The Story, 2. The City, 3. The Citadel, 4. The Writing and 5. The Future.
